In the listing of these homes is a picture of a connected society, in which hearts draw so close that a relative feels at ease in the home of his relative and his friend. Among the beautiful aspects of these bonds is that the family gathers over food, and that the homes of relatives are kept alive with visits. The words “greet one another” (literally, “greet yourselves”) make the greeting of peace the key to every home; so begin with it when you enter, even if the home is your own.

en.title: Seek Help Through Allah and Be Patient
en.excerpt: Musa's advice to his people in a time of hardship: seeking Allah's help, patience, and certainty that the final outcome belongs to the God-conscious.

body.text: Pharaoh's persecution of the Children of Israel intensifies, so Musa (peace be upon him) addresses them with words that steady their hearts, maps out for them the way out of the trial, and reminds them that the earth belongs to Allah, who gives it as inheritance to whom He wills.
قَالَ مُوسَىٰ لِقَوْمِهِ ٱسْتَعِينُوا۟ بِٱللَّهِ وَٱصْبِرُوٓا۟ ۖ إِنَّ ٱلْأَرْضَ لِلَّهِ يُورِثُهَا مَن يَشَآءُ مِنْ عِبَادِهِۦ ۖ وَٱلْعَٰقِبَةُ لِلْمُتَّقِينَ

In hardship a person needs two things: help from Allah, which he draws upon through supplication and reliance, and patience that keeps him from collapsing. Musa (peace be upon him) mentioned seeking help before patience, because patience itself is only achieved with Allah's help. Then he closed with “and the final outcome belongs to the God-conscious”: the trial may be long and the oppressor may rise for a while, but the good ending belongs to the people of taqwa. So when circumstances close in on you, seek Allah's help, be patient, and stay firm on taqwa.

en.title: Why “Praise” and Not “Thanks”?
en.excerpt: Opening Al-Fatihah with the definite “praise” gathers all praise for Allah, for His attributes and His blessings.

body.text: The first thing the reader meets after the basmalah in the Book of Allah is: “All praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds.” A few words, yet they carry the foundations of praising Allah and acknowledging His lordship over all creation.
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ

A subtle insight in the choice of the word “praise” (al-hamd): praise is lauding the one praised for his perfect attributes, even if no kindness from him has reached the one praising, as well as for his blessings; so it is broader than thanks, which is mostly in return for a blessing. It came with the definite article to indicate that the whole of praise, in all its kinds, belongs to Allah. Every true praise ultimately returns to Him.

Then the description “Lord of the worlds” comes to show why He deserves praise: He is the Creator, Nurturer and Disposer of everything besides Him. So whenever you recite it, bring to mind that you are praising a Lord who cares for you and for everything around you. In this way praise becomes a living act of worship, not a passing word.

en.title: If Only I Had Sent Forth for My Life
en.excerpt: The regretful one called the Hereafter his “life,” as if he had known true life only there.

body.text: The two verses depict the Day when Hell is brought forth, and man remembers what he neglected, but of what use is remembrance then, when the time for deeds has passed? He says in sorrow and regret: If only I had sent forth for my life.

وَجِيءَ يَوْمَئِذٍ بِجَهَنَّمَ ۚ يَوْمَئِذٍ يَتَذَكَّرُ الْإِنْسَانُ وَأَنَّىٰ لَهُ الذِّكْرَىٰ
يَقُولُ يَا لَيْتَنِي قَدَّمْتُ لِحَيَاتِي

A subtle insight in the words “sent forth for my life”: he did not say “for my Hereafter”; he made the Hereafter his life, as though what he had lived in the world was not true life. And the expression “sent forth” indicates that deeds are sent ahead of you and you find them there. Reflect on the irony: he remembers when remembrance no longer benefits him. So seize this life of yours to send forth for that life.

en.title: Why Do You Say What You Do Not Do?
en.excerpt: The repetition in the two verses shows how deeply abhorrent it is for words to contradict deeds.

body.text: The verse gently reproaches the believers: why do you say what you do not do? Then it makes clear that this reaches the utmost of hatefulness with Allah. The contradiction between speech and action removes the effect of words and weakens trust.

يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا لِمَ تَقُولُونَ مَا لَا تَفْعَلُونَ
كَبُرَ مَقْتًا عِنْدَ اللَّهِ أَنْ تَقُولُوا مَا لَا تَفْعَلُونَ

A subtle insight in repeating the phrase “what you do not do” in the two verses: the first is a question of reproach, and the second a statement of consequence, and the repetition fixes the meaning in the soul. In the words “greatly hateful” there is an expression of wonder at how great this hatred is, and maqt is the most intense hatred. So do not promise what you will not do, do not speak of virtues you do not practise, and begin with action before words.

en.title: Glory Be to Our Lord; Indeed, We Were Wrongdoers
en.excerpt: The owners of the garden glorified Allah before admitting their wrongdoing: they declared their Lord free of fault, then blamed themselves.

body.text: In the story of the owners of the garden, after what befell their garden because of their resolve to deny the poor, the most just and moderate of them reminded them that he used to call them to glorify Allah. So they said, admitting: Glory be to our Lord; indeed, we were wrongdoers.

قَالَ أَوْسَطُهُمْ أَلَمْ أَقُلْ لَكُمْ لَوْلَا تُسَبِّحُونَ
قَالُوا سُبْحَانَ رَبِّنَا إِنَّا كُنَّا ظَالِمِينَ

A subtle insight in the order: they began by declaring Allah free of imperfection, “Glory be to our Lord,” before saying “indeed, we were wrongdoers,” as if acknowledging that Allah is free of any injustice and that what befell them came from themselves alone. This is a beautiful courtesy in calamity: do not accuse divine decree; rather, glorify your Lord and review yourself, for admitting one's shortcoming is the first step toward reform.

en.title: Then They Did Not Doubt
en.excerpt: True faith is certainty unmixed with doubt, and giving that confirms what is in the heart.

body.text: The verse defines the quality of the truthful believers: they believed in Allah and His Messenger, then their faith was not mixed with doubt, and they strove with their wealth and their lives in the way of Allah; it is they who are the truthful. It makes certainty and giving two signs of true faith.
إِنَّمَا الْمُؤْمِنُونَ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا بِاللَّهِ وَرَسُولِهِ ثُمَّ لَمْ يَرْتَابُوا وَجَاهَدُوا بِأَمْوَالِهِمْ وَأَنْفُسِهِمْ فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ ۚ أُولَٰئِكَ هُمُ الصَّادِقُونَ

The words “then they did not doubt” indicate that faith needs steadfastness after its beginning. Doubts may come to the heart, and the believer repels them with knowledge, remembrance and asking the people of knowledge, and does not let them settle. So look after your certainty as you look after your health.

Linking certainty with giving teaches you that truthfulness is measured by action. So offer something of your wealth, time and effort in good causes, to bear witness to what is in your heart. A little that is constant and sincere is more beloved and more lasting than much that is interrupted.

en.title: And the Best Provision Is Taqwa
en.excerpt: The traveller takes provisions for the road, and the best provision a servant can take on his journey to Allah is taqwa.

body.text: In the context of speaking about Hajj, Allah directs the pilgrims to avoid indecent speech, sinfulness and quarrelling, then commands them to take provisions, and tells them that the best provision is taqwa (God-consciousness). Hajj is a journey of the body and the heart together.

ٱلۡحَجُّ أَشۡهُرٞ مَّعۡلُومَٰتٞۚ فَمَن فَرَضَ فِيهِنَّ ٱلۡحَجَّ فَلَا رَفَثَ وَلَا فُسُوقَ وَلَا جِدَالَ فِي ٱلۡحَجِّۗ وَمَا تَفۡعَلُواْ مِنۡ خَيۡرٖ يَعۡلَمۡهُ ٱللَّهُۗ وَتَزَوَّدُواْ فَإِنَّ خَيۡرَ ٱلزَّادِ ٱلتَّقۡوَىٰۖ وَٱتَّقُونِ يَٰٓأُوْلِي ٱلۡأَلۡبَٰبِ

This meaning goes beyond Hajj to the whole of life: we are all travellers to Allah, every traveller has provisions, and no provision benefits on that journey like taqwa. And in the verse there is reassurance: whatever good we do, “Allah knows it,” so no deed is lost with Him however hidden it may be. So gather your provision from good deeds small and great, and leave the quarrelling that spoils the purity of worship.

en.title: So See What You Think
en.excerpt: Even in a decisive command from Allah, Ibrahim consulted his son, to share the decision with him and make him firm.

body.text: When Isma'il reached the age of working alongside his father, Ibrahim told him of his dream and asked for his view. The son answered with courtesy and steadfastness: Do as you are commanded; you will find me, if Allah wills, among the patient.

فَلَمَّا بَلَغَ مَعَهُ السَّعْيَ قَالَ يَا بُنَيَّ إِنِّي أَرَىٰ فِي الْمَنَامِ أَنِّي أَذْبَحُكَ فَانْظُرْ مَاذَا تَرَىٰ ۚ قَالَ يَا أَبَتِ افْعَلْ مَا تُؤْمَرُ ۖ سَتَجِدُنِي إِنْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ مِنَ الصَّابِرِينَ

In this dialogue there is a lesson in upbringing: to involve our children in matters, listen to their opinions, and treat them with respect, so they grow up with confidence and responsibility. The son's answer shows the fruit of righteous upbringing: conscious obedience, seeking Allah's help, and courtesy in speech. Calm dialogue produces children who carry values out of conviction.

en.title: I Only Desire Reform as Much as I Am Able
en.excerpt: Shu'ayb combines a truthful example, the will to reform, and reliance on Allah for success.

body.text: Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) addresses his people, who used to give short measure and weight, and makes clear to them that he does not command them to do something and then do the opposite himself, and that his goal is reform to the extent of his ability. These are words fit to be the motto of every reformer.

قَالَ يَا قَوْمِ أَرَأَيْتُمْ إِنْ كُنْتُ عَلَىٰ بَيِّنَةٍ مِنْ رَبِّي وَرَزَقَنِي مِنْهُ رِزْقًا حَسَنًا ۚ وَمَا أُرِيدُ أَنْ أُخَالِفَكُمْ إِلَىٰ مَا أَنْهَاكُمْ عَنْهُ ۚ إِنْ أُرِيدُ إِلَّا الْإِصْلَاحَ مَا اسْتَطَعْتُ ۚ وَمَا تَوْفِيقِي إِلَّا بِاللَّهِ ۚ عَلَيْهِ تَوَكَّلْتُ وَإِلَيْهِ أُنِيبُ

Whoever wants to reform others should begin with himself, and not say what he does not do. Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) made the consistency of his words and deeds proof of the truth of his call. Then he set his goal realistically, “as much as I am able,” and attributed all success to Allah. So do not burden yourself beyond your capacity in reforming those around you; work within your means, rely on Allah, and turn back to Him often.

en.title: They Plan, and Allah Plans
en.excerpt: Setting the scheming of the obstinate against Allah's planning reveals that human plotting is encompassed by His power.

body.text: The verse recalls a moment when the obstinate gathered to plot against the Prophet ﷺ: to imprison him, kill him or expel him, and the divine answer at its close was decisive. In it is a great lesson for everyone who is wronged.
وَإِذۡ يَمۡكُرُ بِكَ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُواْ لِيُثۡبِتُوكَ أَوۡ يَقۡتُلُوكَ أَوۡ يُخۡرِجُوكَۚ وَيَمۡكُرُونَ وَيَمۡكُرُ ٱللَّهُۖ وَٱللَّهُ خَيۡرُ ٱلۡمَٰكِرِينَ

A subtle insight in the contrast between “they plan” and “Allah plans”: both verbs came in the present tense, indicating renewal, so that whenever they devised a plot, Allah's planning encompassed it and turned it back upon them. Allah's planning is a hidden arrangement against His enemies befitting His majesty, and it is justice and wisdom. No plot takes effect except by His permission.

Then the verse closes with “and Allah is the best of planners,” meaning the best and most effective in planning. So the believer is reassured that whatever injustice is plotted against him does not lie outside Allah's knowledge and disposal. Let his heart be at peace, and let him stand firm on the truth.

en.title: That I Might Do Righteousness in What I Left Behind
en.excerpt: At death the negligent one wishes neither for wealth nor family, but for a respite in which to do good.

body.text: The two verses describe the state of one whom death comes to while he has been negligent. He asks his Lord to send him back to the world so that he might do righteousness in what he left behind, and the decisive answer comes to him as a rebuke: behind them is a barrier until the Day they are resurrected.

حَتَّىٰٓ إِذَا جَآءَ أَحَدَهُمُ ٱلْمَوْتُ قَالَ رَبِّ ٱرْجِعُونِ
لَعَلِّىٓ أَعْمَلُ صَٰلِحًۭا فِيمَا تَرَكْتُ ۚ كَلَّآ ۚ إِنَّهَا كَلِمَةٌ هُوَ قَآئِلُهَا ۖ وَمِن وَرَآئِهِم بَرْزَخٌ إِلَىٰ يَوْمِ يُبْعَثُونَ

A subtle insight in the dying person's wish: he did not ask to return to enjoy or to accumulate, but to do righteousness. When reality is unveiled, it becomes clear that deeds are the only thing of value. The words “it is but a word he utters” indicate that it is a word that goes no further than his tongue and will not be granted. What the negligent one wishes for there is available to you here, now.

en.title: And Indeed, You Are of a Great Moral Character
en.excerpt: The preposition “upon” portrays great character as a firm station on which its possessor stands.

body.text: A divine testimony for our Prophet Muhammad ﷺ that he is of a great moral character, confirmed with more than one form of emphasis, so that it is the greatest commendation of his character and the clearest call to us to follow his example in dealing with people.
وَإِنَّكَ لَعَلَىٰ خُلُقٍ عَظِيمٍ

A subtle insight in choosing the preposition of elevation in “upon a great character” (la-'ala khuluqin 'azim), rather than saying “possessing character”: it portrays character as a steady mount that its possessor rides upon and is in full command of, not a passing trait. The verse brings together the particle of emphasis and the emphatic lam, and the Almighty Himself describes it as great. Whoever wishes to follow his example should make good character a permanent station, not a temporary state.

en.title: So Glory Be to Him in Whose Hand Is the Dominion of All Things
en.excerpt: Surah Ya-Sin ends with glorification after speaking of Allah's power to resurrect and create.

body.text: This verse comes at the close of Surah Ya-Sin, after showing Allah's power to give life to the dead and to create the heavens and the earth. It declares the perfection of Allah, in whose hand is the dominion of all things and their disposal, and to whom creation returns.
فَسُبۡحَٰنَ ٱلَّذِي بِيَدِهِۦ مَلَكُوتُ كُلِّ شَيۡءٖ وَإِلَيۡهِ تُرۡجَعُونَ

A subtle insight in the word “malakut” (dominion): it is an intensive form of mulk (sovereignty), denoting complete and vast sovereignty, and it comes with “all things” to include everything small and great. Then the “so” in “So glory be” comes as a conclusion from the preceding proofs, as though glorification is the natural fruit of reflecting on Allah's power. So when you contemplate the greatness of creation, let your tongue glorify Him, for this is the hoped-for fruit of reflection.

en.title: Indeed, I Am Going to My Lord; He Will Guide Me
en.excerpt: When you leave what you are used to, seeking Allah's pleasure, trust that He will guide you to what is better.

body.text: Allah relates that Ibrahim said: I am emigrating to my Lord, leaving the land of my people so that I can worship Him, and my Lord will guide me to what is good for me in this world and the Hereafter.
وَقَالَ إِنِّي ذَاهِبٌ إِلَىٰ رَبِّي سَيَهْدِينِ

His words “going to my Lord” make every transition in life a journey to Allah when the intention is sound. Changing company, leaving a habit, or starting a new path can be a going to Allah. So in your major decisions, make your intention the seeking of His pleasure.

And his words “He will guide me” express certainty about the future even when its features are not yet clear. Ibrahim did not know the details of what awaited him, but he trusted his Lord. So when you take a step in obedience to Allah, do not let uncertainty worry you, and ask Him for guidance at every stage.

en.title: Those Whose Hearts Tremble When Allah Is Mentioned
en.excerpt: Four qualities of the humble: a heart that trembles, patience in trial, established prayer, and constant spending.

body.text: In Surah Al-Hajj, after speaking of the rites, this verse describes those who humble themselves before Allah: their hearts are filled with awe when Allah is mentioned, they are patient with what befalls them, they establish prayer, and they spend from what Allah has provided them.
الَّذِينَ إِذَا ذُكِرَ اللَّهُ وَجِلَتْ قُلُوبُهُمْ وَالصَّابِرِينَ عَلَىٰ مَا أَصَابَهُمْ وَالْمُقِيمِي الصَّلَاةِ وَمِمَّا رَزَقْنَاهُمْ يُنْفِقُونَ

Notice that the qualities begin with the heart, then move to patience, then prayer, then spending. Outward worship is the fruit of a living heart that is moved by the remembrance of Allah. So test your heart when you hear the Qur'an or the mention of Allah: does it soften and become humble? If you find it hard, increase in remembrance and prayer until it softens, for the heart learns humility through constancy.

en.title: And Their Affairs Are Conducted by Mutual Consultation
en.excerpt: Consultation is a deep-rooted trait of the believing community, and it begins at home before anywhere else.

body.text: Among the qualities of the believers, the verse mentions that they responded to their Lord, established prayer, conduct their affairs by consultation among themselves, and spend from what Allah has provided them. Consultation thus comes in this context between two great acts of worship: prayer and spending.
وَالَّذِينَ اسْتَجَابُوا لِرَبِّهِمْ وَأَقَامُوا الصَّلَاةَ وَأَمْرُهُمْ شُورَىٰ بَيْنَهُمْ وَمِمَّا رَزَقْنَاهُمْ يُنْفِقُونَ

A home whose decisions are made through consultation between the spouses, and in which the children's opinions are heard, is a home with fewer disputes and more contentment. So set a family session in which you consult one another on your affairs: travel, spending or education. Sharing in a decision increases commitment to it and strengthens the bonds of love.

en.title: Indeed, Whoever Fears Allah and Is Patient
en.excerpt: Yusuf turned his personal story into a general rule for everyone who fears Allah and is patient.

body.text: In the moving moment of reunion, Yusuf (peace be upon him) reveals himself to his brothers. He does not speak of his intelligence or his planning; rather he attributes the favour to Allah, and draws from the whole experience a lesson that goes beyond himself.
قَالُوا أَإِنَّكَ لَأَنْتَ يُوسُفُ ۖ قَالَ أَنَا يُوسُفُ وَهَٰذَا أَخِي ۖ قَدْ مَنَّ اللَّهُ عَلَيْنَا ۖ إِنَّهُ مَنْ يَتَّقِ وَيَصْبِرْ فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ لَا يُضِيعُ أَجْرَ الْمُحْسِنِينَ

A subtle insight in the expression: Yusuf said, “Allah has been gracious to us,” then moved directly to a general form, “Indeed, whoever fears Allah and is patient.” He did not make his story an exception, but an example of a constant divine law that applies to everyone who combines taqwa and patience. Then he closed with “Allah does not let the reward of those who do good be lost,” calling the God-fearing and patient “those who do good,” as though taqwa and patience together are the reality of ihsan. This gives everyone being tested certainty that his patience is not wasted.

en.title: From Between Digested Matter and Blood, Pure Milk
en.excerpt: Describing milk as pure after mentioning digested matter and blood makes the miracle present in every day's glass.

body.text: The verse presents a lesson people pass by every day: milk that comes from livestock, which they drink with ease, yet it is produced in a place between waste and blood, and then reaches them pure and delicious.
وَإِنَّ لَكُمْ فِي الْأَنْعَامِ لَعِبْرَةً ۖ نُسْقِيكُمْ مِمَّا فِي بُطُونِهِ مِنْ بَيْنِ فَرْثٍ وَدَمٍ لَبَنًا خَالِصًا سَائِغًا لِلشَّارِبِينَ

A subtle insight in the order of descriptions: “digested matter and blood” is mentioned first so the listener recalls the place it comes from, then “pure milk” follows, and the contrast has a striking effect. Then it adds “palatable to drinkers,” meaning easy to swallow, so the verse combines purity of substance with pleasure of taste. How wondrous is this precise divine making!

And He said “We give you to drink,” attributing the giving of drink to Himself, to remind you that the glass of milk on your table is drink given by Allah, and that in livestock there is “a lesson” for the one who reflects, not for the one who merely drinks. A lesson needs a heart that contemplates.

en.title: And There Will Remain the Face of Your Lord
en.excerpt: The Qur'an contrasts perishing with remaining in order to attach the heart to the One who remains alone.

body.text: Two short verses place all existence on a scale: everyone upon the earth will perish, and there will remain the Face of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honour, who neither passes away nor changes, and to whom all creatures return.

كُلُّ مَنْ عَلَيْهَا فَانٍ
وَيَبْقَىٰ وَجْهُ رَبِّكَ ذُو الْجَلَالِ وَالْإِكْرَامِ

A subtle insight in the contrast between “everyone upon it will perish,” expressed with a noun form indicating fixity, and “and there will remain the Face of your Lord,” expressed with a present-tense verb indicating continuity: perishing is an inseparable trait of creation, and remaining belongs permanently to Allah. And closing with Majesty and Honour combines greatness and kindness. Whoever attaches himself to the One who remains will not be devastated by the loss of what perishes.

en.title: A Kind Word and Forgiveness
en.excerpt: A kind word with pardon is better than a charity followed by hurt.

body.text: The verse compares two things: a kind word with overlooking the one who asks, and a charity followed by hurt through reminders of favour or wounding words. It makes the kind word better, because a person's dignity is more precious than money that hurts.
قَوۡلٞ مَّعۡرُوفٞ وَمَغۡفِرَةٌ خَيۡرٞ مِّن صَدَقَةٖ يَتۡبَعُهَآ أَذٗىۗ وَٱللَّهُ غَنِيٌّ حَلِيمٞ

A subtle insight in closing the verse with “and Allah is Free of need, Forbearing”: He has no need of a charity accompanied by hurt; and He is Forbearing, not hastening to punish the one who hurts, but giving him respite to repent. The two names together combine a rebuke for the one who reminds of his favours with an open door to return. So when you give, give with dignity, and if you find nothing to give, say a kind word.

en.title: My Lord, Do Not Leave Me Alone, and You Are the Best of Inheritors
en.excerpt: Zakariyya ended his request for a child by praising Allah as the best of inheritors, out of courtesy and surrender.

body.text: Allah mentions His Prophet Zakariyya (peace be upon him) when he called upon his Lord, asking Him not to leave him alone without a child to inherit from him the mission and knowledge. Then he closed his supplication by praising Allah as the best of inheritors, so Allah answered him and granted him Yahya.
وَزَكَرِيَّآ إِذۡ نَادَىٰ رَبَّهُۥ رَبِّ لَا تَذَرۡنِي فَرۡدٗا وَأَنتَ خَيۡرُ ٱلۡوَٰرِثِينَ

A subtle insight in the ending: Zakariyya asked for an heir, then closed with “and You are the best of inheritors,” as if saying: if You grant me a child, that is from Your grace, and if You do not, You are the best of those who inherit, so I do not fear that what I carry will be lost. He combined request with surrender. This is how supplication should be: sincere longing together with contentment with what Allah decrees, and choosing the name you call upon to suit your need.

en.title: He Is Allah, Besides Whom There Is No God
en.excerpt: Repeating “He is Allah” in three successive verses fixes in the heart the greatness of the One named.

body.text: Surah Al-Hashr closes with three verses that all begin with “He is Allah,” in which the most beautiful names follow one another: Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful, the King, the Most Holy, the Source of Peace, the Creator, the Originator, the Fashioner. They end with the glorification of Him by all that is in the heavens and the earth.

هُوَ اللَّهُ الَّذِي لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ ۖ عَالِمُ الْغَيْبِ وَالشَّهَادَةِ ۖ هُوَ الرَّحْمَٰنُ الرَّحِيمُ
هُوَ اللَّهُ الَّذِي لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا هُوَ الْمَلِكُ الْقُدُّوسُ السَّلَامُ الْمُؤْمِنُ الْمُهَيْمِنُ الْعَزِيزُ الْجَبَّارُ الْمُتَكَبِّرُ ۚ سُبْحَانَ اللَّهِ عَمَّا يُشْرِكُونَ
هُوَ اللَّهُ الْخَالِقُ الْبَارِئُ الْمُصَوِّرُ ۖ لَهُ الْأَسْمَاءُ الْحُسْنَىٰ ۚ يُسَبِّحُ لَهُ مَا فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ ۖ وَهُوَ الْعَزِيزُ الْحَكِيمُ

A subtle insight in repeating “He is Allah” at the start of each verse: it is a repetition that knocks on the heart again and again, as though each verse opens a new window onto Allah's greatness, so the listener grows in knowledge and reverence with every name.

Notice how the names begin with His knowledge and mercy, then His sovereignty and holiness, then His creating and fashioning, and close with “to Him belong the most beautiful names.” So make these names the substance of your supplication, asking by each name what suits it, and reflect on their meanings with a present heart.

en.title: A Decree of Specified Times
en.excerpt: “Has been,” “a decree” and “of specified times”: three words describing the standing and constancy of prayer.

body.text: This verse commands remembering Allah standing, sitting and lying on one's side after completing the prayer, then commands establishing it once in security, and closes by stating its status: that it has been upon the believers a decree of specified times.

فَإِذَا قَضَيْتُمُ الصَّلَاةَ فَاذْكُرُوا اللَّهَ قِيَامًا وَقُعُودًا وَعَلَىٰ جُنُوبِكُمْ ۚ فَإِذَا اطْمَأْنَنْتُمْ فَأَقِيمُوا الصَّلَاةَ ۚ إِنَّ الصَّلَاةَ كَانَتْ عَلَى الْمُؤْمِنِينَ كِتَابًا مَوْقُوتًا

A subtle insight in the word “has been” (kanat): it indicates that prayer is a fixed and settled obligation that does not fall away with changing circumstances. “A decree” (kitaban) carries the meaning of a written, firmly established obligation, and “of specified times” (mawqutan) that it has set times; it is as though prayer is a series of regular appointments that Allah sets for His servants in their day. And in mentioning remembrance after the prayer in every posture is an indication that the prayer ends with the salam, but remembrance never ends.

en.title: O My Dear Son, Do Not Associate Partners with Allah
en.excerpt: The call “O my dear son,” in its diminutive form, carries a father's tenderness before it carries his advice.

body.text: The Qur'an relates the counsel of Luqman the Wise to his son. He opens it with a tender call full of compassion, then begins with the greatest issue and the one most deserving of priority: the prohibition of associating partners with Allah, and the explanation that it is a tremendous wrong by which a person wrongs himself.
وَإِذْ قَالَ لُقْمَانُ لِابْنِهِ وَهُوَ يَعِظُهُ يَا بُنَيَّ لَا تُشْرِكْ بِاللَّهِ ۖ إِنَّ الشِّرْكَ لَظُلْمٌ عَظِيمٌ

A subtle insight in the words “O my dear son” (ya bunayya): the call came in the diminutive form, which expresses endearment and compassion, not belittlement. It is as if the father says to his son: you are close to my heart, and what I say comes from my love for you. And in the words “while he was advising him” is an indication that advising was an ongoing state, not a passing word. Whoever wants his advice to be heard should begin it with love, and be patient with repeating it gently.

en.title: I Have Encompassed That Which You Have Not
en.excerpt: A small bird addresses a mighty king with confidence: I have knowledge that you do not.

body.text: The hoopoe is absent from the assembly of Sulayman (peace be upon him), so he threatens it. Then it returns after a short while, begins its speech with a bold statement, and brings certain news about the people of Saba'. In its words are subtleties worth reflecting on.
فَمَكَثَ غَيْرَ بَعِيدٍ فَقَالَ أَحَطْتُ بِمَا لَمْ تُحِطْ بِهِ وَجِئْتُكَ مِنْ سَبَإٍ بِنَبَإٍ يَقِينٍ

A subtle insight in the expression: the small hoopoe said to a prophet-king, “I have encompassed that which you have not encompassed.” Knowledge is not monopolised by the great or by those in authority; the small may have what the great do not. And Sulayman (peace be upon him) listened to it and was not arrogant.

Reflect on the wordplay in “from Saba' with certain news” (min Saba'in bi-naba'in yaqin): the two words are close in sound but different in meaning, and the news is described as “certain” to show that it had verified it. In this is a lesson in etiquette for whoever conveys news: to verify before speaking.

en.title: And Your Lord Inspired the Bee
en.excerpt: The expressions “inspired” and “paths made easy” reveal how Allah guides the smallest of His creatures to what benefits them.

body.text: The two verses describe how Allah guided the bee to take its dwellings in the mountains, the trees and what people construct, then to eat from all the fruits, and then there emerges from their bellies a drink of varying colours in which there is healing for people.

وَأَوْحَىٰ رَبُّكَ إِلَى النَّحْلِ أَنِ اتَّخِذِي مِنَ الْجِبَالِ بُيُوتًا وَمِنَ الشَّجَرِ وَمِمَّا يَعْرِشُونَ
ثُمَّ كُلِي مِنْ كُلِّ الثَّمَرَاتِ فَاسْلُكِي سُبُلَ رَبِّكِ ذُلُلًا ۚ يَخْرُجُ مِنْ بُطُونِهَا شَرَابٌ مُخْتَلِفٌ أَلْوَانُهُ فِيهِ شِفَاءٌ لِلنَّاسِ ۗ إِنَّ فِي ذَٰلِكَ لَآيَةً لِقَوْمٍ يَتَفَكَّرُونَ

A subtle insight in the expression “inspired” (awha): what is meant here is instinctive inspiration and guidance, and choosing this word conveys Allah's care for this small creature. Then He said “the paths of your Lord,” attributing the paths to Himself, and described them as “made easy,” meaning smoothed for it, so the bee travels along paths its Lord has prepared for it. How great is this arrangement for a small creature! So when you taste honey, remember that it is your Lord who guided the bee to make it, and that divine wisdom encompasses every atom in this universe.

The verse closes with “for people who reflect.” Everyone sees honey, but the sign in it is perceived only by those who reflect on this precise guidance. Others eat it heedless of this sign; so be among those who reflect, who see in every blessing evidence of the Giver of blessings, glory be to Him.

en.title: Mankind's Reckoning Has Drawn Near
en.excerpt: The verb came in the past tense to make you feel that the nearness has already occurred, while people are heedless.

body.text: Surah Al-Anbiya opens with an awe-inspiring warning that shakes hearts: the time of people's reckoning for their deeds has drawn near, yet they are heedless of this Day, turning away from preparing for it and reflecting on it.
ٱقۡتَرَبَ لِلنَّاسِ حِسَابُهُمۡ وَهُمۡ فِي غَفۡلَةٖ مُّعۡرِضُونَ

A subtle insight in the wording “Mankind's reckoning has drawn near”: the verb came in the past tense as though the nearness were already accomplished, and the additional letters in the verb (iqtaraba) indicate intensity of nearness. The reckoning is attributed to them so that each person feels the matter concerns him. Then the verse combines heedlessness and turning away: heedlessness is forgetting, and turning away is turning one's back while knowing, and both are diseases that need awakening.

en.title: And Do Not Defame Yourselves
en.excerpt: Whoever finds fault with his brother has, as it were, found fault with himself, for the believers are one body.

body.text: The verse forbids mocking others, for perhaps the one mocked is better than the mocker, and it forbids defaming and calling one another by offensive nicknames, because these are acts that wound hearts, spoil brotherhood and sow enmity among people.

يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا لَا يَسْخَرْ قَوْمٌ مِنْ قَوْمٍ عَسَىٰ أَنْ يَكُونُوا خَيْرًا مِنْهُمْ وَلَا نِسَاءٌ مِنْ نِسَاءٍ عَسَىٰ أَنْ يَكُنَّ خَيْرًا مِنْهُنَّ ۖ وَلَا تَلْمِزُوا أَنْفُسَكُمْ وَلَا تَنَابَزُوا بِالْأَلْقَابِ ۖ بِئْسَ الِاسْمُ الْفُسُوقُ بَعْدَ الْإِيمَانِ ۚ وَمَنْ لَمْ يَتُبْ فَأُولَٰئِكَ هُمُ الظَّالِمُونَ

A subtle insight in the words “and do not defame yourselves”: He did not say “do not defame others”; rather He made the believer who is criticised as though he were the very self of the critic, because the believers are like one body, and whoever attacks his brother has attacked himself. And in the words “perhaps they may be better” is a reminder that appearances are deceptive, and the scales with Allah are by taqwa.

en.title: Our Lord, We Have Wronged Ourselves
en.excerpt: The supplication of Adam and his wife came in the plural: they shared in the admission without either blaming the other.

body.text: After Adam and his wife ate from the tree, they did not look for an excuse. Rather, they admitted together that they had done wrong, asked Allah for forgiveness and mercy, and said that if He did not forgive them they would be among the losers.
قَالَا رَبَّنَا ظَلَمْنَآ أَنفُسَنَا وَإِن لَّمْ تَغْفِرْ لَنَا وَتَرْحَمْنَا لَنَكُونَنَّ مِنَ ٱلْخَٰسِرِينَ

A subtle insight in the forms “they both said” and “we have wronged”: the admission came jointly, with the dual and plural pronouns, and neither blamed the other. They placed forgiveness before mercy, because first erasing the sin paves the way for mercy to descend after it. In this is a lesson for the family: when a mistake is shared, spouses do not trade accusations; they return to Allah together in repentance.

en.title: Hidden by Night and Going About by Day
en.excerpt: The one hiding in the darkness of night and the one visible in broad daylight are alike in Allah's knowledge.

body.text: The verse affirms that in Allah's knowledge it is the same whether one conceals speech or declares it, and whether one is hidden by the darkness of night or out in the open, going on his way by day.
سَوَاءٌ مِنْكُمْ مَنْ أَسَرَّ الْقَوْلَ وَمَنْ جَهَرَ بِهِ وَمَنْ هُوَ مُسْتَخْفٍ بِاللَّيْلِ وَسَارِبٌ بِالنَّهَارِ

A subtle insight in the verse being built on contrasts: “conceals” and “declares,” then “hidden by night” and “going about by day.” It brings together words and deeds, concealment and openness, and both times, so that no state of a person remains outside Allah's knowledge.

And in choosing the word “alike” at the start of the verse is an indication that what differs for people in terms of hiddenness and visibility does not differ for Allah. So let your private and public life also be alike in righteousness, for whoever finds the two states alike is relieved of putting on a show before people.

en.title: And Prostrate and Draw Near
en.excerpt: Allah joined prostration with drawing near, for the servant is closest to his Lord when he is prostrating.

body.text: Surah Al-'Alaq closes with two short commands, “and prostrate and draw near,” after forbidding obedience to the one who obstructs the prayer. The answer to obstruction and tyranny was a prostration by which the servant draws near to his Lord.
كَلَّا لَا تُطِعْهُ وَٱسْجُدْ وَٱقْتَرِب ۩

A subtle insight in joining “draw near” to “prostrate” without separation: it is as though prostration itself is the path to nearness, and as though every time the servant places his forehead on the ground, his standing with Allah is raised. The lowest place of the body is the highest station. Notice the brevity of the phrase: just two words that sum up the whole journey of servitude, humility with the body and nearness with the soul. So when you prostrate, lengthen your prostration, and speak intimately to your Lord in it of what is in your heart.

en.title: As Brothers, on Thrones Facing One Another
en.excerpt: In Paradise no brother turns his back on his brother: faces are turned toward one another and hearts are pure.

body.text: The verse describes the people of Paradise: Allah has removed whatever rancour was in their chests, so they have become brothers sitting on thrones facing one another, looking at each other in purity and intimacy.
وَنَزَعْنَا مَا فِي صُدُورِهِمْ مِنْ غِلٍّ إِخْوَانًا عَلَىٰ سُرُرٍ مُتَقَابِلِينَ

A subtle insight in the order of the verse: it mentions the removal of rancour before mentioning brotherhood and the gatherings, indicating that brotherhood is not complete while hearts carry grudges, and that a pure chest is the foundation of all intimacy. The word “facing one another” paints a beautiful picture: no one turns his back on anyone. So bring something of this into your family gatherings: faces turned toward each other, sound hearts, and continual cleansing of the chests.

en.title: So I Intended to Cause Defect in It
en.excerpt: The righteous servant attributed the intention of causing the defect to himself, out of courtesy in mentioning what outwardly seems bad.

body.text: The righteous servant begins explaining what he did to the ship he holed: it belonged to poor people who worked at sea, and ahead of them was a king who seized every ship by force. In the wording of this explanation is a fine courtesy.
أَمَّا ٱلسَّفِينَةُ فَكَانَتۡ لِمَسَٰكِينَ يَعۡمَلُونَ فِي ٱلۡبَحۡرِ فَأَرَدتُّ أَنۡ أَعِيبَهَا وَكَانَ وَرَآءَهُم مَّلِكٞ يَأۡخُذُ كُلَّ سَفِينَةٍ غَصۡبٗا

A subtle insight in how the act is attributed: he said, “So I intended to cause defect in it,” attributing the defect to himself, even though he did it by Allah's command, out of courtesy so that what outwardly appears as a deficiency is not attributed to Allah. The verse also calls them “poor” even though they owned a ship.

A poor person may own something that does not suffice him, and a small defect may be the cause of preserving the whole thing from loss. How many a deficiency we see in our lives contains a hidden kindness from Allah that we only grasp after some time.

en.title: And by the Dawn When It Breathes
en.excerpt: Depicting the dawn as breathing brings life and relief into the scene after the darkness of night.

body.text: Allah swears by the night as it approaches with its darkness, or departs, and by the dawn when it breathes: two successive scenes every person knows, but the Qur'anic expression gives them new life. Reflect on how the Qur'an depicts this moment.

وَاللَّيْلِ إِذَا عَسْعَسَ
وَالصُّبْحِ إِذَا تَنَفَّسَ

A subtle insight in the metaphor: the dawn is made like a living being that breathes. The coming of light and the spreading of the breeze at the start of the day resemble a deep breath after long holding it in. In this is a suggestion of relief and ease after the heaviness of darkness.

In this scene is a message for troubled souls: just as dawn comes after night, relief comes after hardship. So when you see the light of dawn, remember that Allah, who brings forth day from night, is able to bring you out of your worry.

en.title: Allah Will Replace Their Evil Deeds with Good Deeds
en.excerpt: He did not say only that He erases their evil deeds, but that He replaces them with good deeds; this is the height of generosity.

body.text: After Allah mentioned the major sins and their consequence, He made an exception for whoever repents, believes and does righteous deeds, and gave them the glad tidings that Allah will replace their evil deeds with good deeds. And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful to His repentant servants.
إِلَّا مَن تَابَ وَءَامَنَ وَعَمِلَ عَمَلٗا صَٰلِحٗا فَأُوْلَٰٓئِكَ يُبَدِّلُ ٱللَّهُ سَيِّـَٔاتِهِمۡ حَسَنَٰتٖۗ وَكَانَ ٱللَّهُ غَفُورٗا رَّحِيمٗا

A subtle insight in the expression of replacement: pardon is the erasing of a sin, and replacement is beyond that, as it puts a good deed in the place of the evil one. The verse sets three conditions: repentance, faith and righteous deeds, for repentance is not a word spoken but a transformation of life. And it closes with “Forgiving and Merciful” to reassure hearts weighed down by the past.

en.title: Woe to Every Slanderer and Backbiter
en.excerpt: The form fu'alah denotes one in whom fault-finding has become a firmly rooted habit.

body.text: The surah begins with a warning to those who habitually find fault with people and attack them by word or gesture. It is a trait that ruins relationships, spreads hatred, and makes its owner disliked by Allah and by people, however much he thinks he is joking or offering good criticism.
وَيْلٌ لِكُلِّ هُمَزَةٍ لُمَزَةٍ

A subtle insight in the form of humazah lumazah, on the pattern fu'alah: it is an intensive form indicating frequency of the act until it becomes a constant habit. What is meant is not a passing slip, but an entrenched trait. The two words are close in pattern and sound, so they strike the ear. So beware of letting criticism of people become your habit, and watch your tongue, your gestures and your facial expressions.

en.title: My Lord, I Seek Refuge in You from Asking You That of Which I Have No Knowledge
en.excerpt: Nuh sought refuge in Allah from supplication itself when it is not based on knowledge, and this is among the finest etiquettes of supplication.

body.text: After Nuh (peace be upon him) asked his Lord concerning his son who drowned, and Allah made the reality of the matter clear to him, Nuh immediately turned back, seeking refuge in Allah from asking Him that of which he had no knowledge, and asked for forgiveness and mercy.
قَالَ رَبِّ إِنِّي أَعُوذُ بِكَ أَنْ أَسْأَلَكَ مَا لَيْسَ لِي بِهِ عِلْمٌ ۖ وَإِلَّا تَغْفِرْ لِي وَتَرْحَمْنِي أَكُنْ مِنَ الْخَاسِرِينَ

A subtle insight in this seeking of refuge: one usually seeks refuge from evil, but Nuh sought refuge from a request whose outcome he did not know, making supplication itself a place for scrupulousness. He began with “My Lord” as a close call without the vocative “O,” indicating the nearness of the supplicant to his Lord. So learn to ask Allah for the good that He knows, and to submit to Him in what you do not know the wisdom of.

en.title: And You Are the Most Merciful of the Merciful
en.excerpt: Ayyub supplicated by describing his state and mentioning his Lord's mercy, and the answer came with more than he asked.

body.text: The two verses mention the supplication of Ayyub when his affliction intensified: “Indeed, adversity has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful.” Then Allah answered him by removing his adversity and giving him his family and the like of them with them, as a mercy and a reminder for the worshippers.

وَأَيُّوبَ إِذۡ نَادَىٰ رَبَّهُۥٓ أَنِّي مَسَّنِيَ ٱلضُّرُّ وَأَنتَ أَرۡحَمُ ٱلرَّٰحِمِينَ
فَٱسۡتَجَبۡنَا لَهُۥ فَكَشَفۡنَا مَا بِهِۦ مِن ضُرّٖۖ وَءَاتَيۡنَٰهُ أَهۡلَهُۥ وَمِثۡلَهُم مَّعَهُمۡ رَحۡمَةٗ مِّنۡ عِندِنَا وَذِكۡرَىٰ لِلۡعَٰبِدِينَ

A subtle insight in the etiquette of this supplication: Ayyub did not say “remove it from me”; he described his state, “adversity has touched me,” and praised his Lord, “and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful,” leaving the request to be understood from the situation. In this is a lesson in gentleness in supplication and beautiful praise.

Then the answer came with the “so” of immediate sequence, “So We answered him... and removed,” indicating the speed of the response. Added to the removal of adversity was “and the like of them with them,” and it closed with “a reminder for the worshippers” so that every worshipper knows this door is open to him, and that patience bears fruit.

en.title: Indeed, the Recitation at Dawn Is Ever Witnessed
en.excerpt: Allah called the dawn prayer “recitation” (qur'an), indicating the length of recitation in it and its virtue.

body.text: This verse gathers the times of prayer in a concise phrase, from the sun's decline to the darkness of night, then singles out the dawn prayer for mention and describes it as witnessed. In its words are rhetorical secrets worth reflecting on.
أَقِمِ الصَّلَاةَ لِدُلُوكِ الشَّمْسِ إِلَىٰ غَسَقِ اللَّيْلِ وَقُرْآنَ الْفَجْرِ ۖ إِنَّ قُرْآنَ الْفَجْرِ كَانَ مَشْهُودًا

A subtle insight in calling the dawn prayer “the recitation of dawn” (qur'an al-fajr): the prayer is expressed by its most prominent element, recitation, to draw attention to the special status of the Qur'an at dawn. Then the same phrase is repeated, “Indeed, the recitation of dawn,” rather than “indeed, it,” and the repetition adds to its glorification and evokes longing.

In describing it as “witnessed” is an indication that this time has a special presence and witnessing. So be keen that you too witness the dawn prayer, and listen in it to the words of Allah with a clear heart at the start of the day.

en.title: My Lord, Forgive Me and My Brother
en.excerpt: After a moment of anger at his brother, the first thing Musa did was pray for him.

body.text: After Musa returned to his people angry and seized his brother Harun by the head, Harun's excuse became clear to him, so he turned to his Lord asking forgiveness for himself and his brother, and that He admit them both into His mercy.
قَالَ رَبِّ ٱغْفِرْ لِى وَلِأَخِى وَأَدْخِلْنَا فِى رَحْمَتِكَ ۖ وَأَنتَ أَرْحَمُ ٱلرَّٰحِمِينَ

A subtle insight in the shift from anger to supplication: Musa did not merely apologise; he included his brother with himself in asking for forgiveness, erasing the trace of harshness with mercy. His words “and admit us,” with the plural pronoun, place the two brothers within one mercy, and he closed with “and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful.” So if you are harsh with a relative, follow it with a supplication that brings you together with him.

en.title: It Is My Staff; I Lean upon It
en.excerpt: Musa was asked a short question about his staff, and he lengthened his answer, finding comfort in conversing with his Lord.

body.text: In the sacred valley, Allah asks Musa (peace be upon him) what is in his right hand, though He, glory be to Him, knows best. Musa gives a detailed answer, mentioning the uses of his staff one after another.

وَمَا تِلْكَ بِيَمِينِكَ يَا مُوسَىٰ
قَالَ هِيَ عَصَايَ أَتَوَكَّأُ عَلَيْهَا وَأَهُشُّ بِهَا عَلَىٰ غَنَمِي وَلِيَ فِيهَا مَآرِبُ أُخْرَىٰ

A subtle insight in the answer: it would have sufficed to say “It is my staff,” but he added that he leans on it and beats down leaves with it for his sheep, then said, “and I have other uses for it.” It is as though he loved for the conversation to be prolonged in this station of intimate address.

Then at the end of his words he summarised and did not detail the “other uses,” out of courtesy and for fear of going on too long. He combined delight in speaking with his Lord with the courtesy of stopping at the limit. And the question was a preparation for what would later happen with the staff.

en.title: Read, and Your Lord Is the Most Generous
en.excerpt: Describing Allah as the Most Generous in the context of reading and teaching makes knowledge one of the greatest forms of His generosity.

body.text: Among the earliest revelations of the Qur'an, the command to read comes joined with the description of the Lord as the Most Generous, who taught by the pen, taught man what he did not know. In this pairing is a subtle meaning worth reflecting on.

ٱقْرَأْ وَرَبُّكَ ٱلْأَكْرَمُ
ٱلَّذِى عَلَّمَ بِٱلْقَلَمِ
عَلَّمَ ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ مَا لَمْ يَعْلَمْ

A subtle insight in the form “the Most Generous” (al-Akram): it comes in the superlative, meaning the One whom no generous one approaches in generosity, and it comes in the context of teaching to show that among the noblest forms of generosity is that Allah teaches man. Then He mentioned “taught by the pen” before “taught man,” drawing attention first to the means and then to the goal.

Every piece of knowledge you learn is from your Lord's generosity to you; so meet it with gratitude, use it for good, and begin your reading and learning in His name, as the surah began. Make your knowledge a path to knowing your Lord, the Most Generous, and drawing near to Him, for knowledge that does not bring one closer to Allah is lacking in blessing.

en.title: Wary of the Hereafter and Hoping for the Mercy of His Lord
en.excerpt: Wariness is attached to the Hereafter, and hope to the Lord's mercy; so fear and hope come together in the heart.

body.text: The verse describes a devoutly obedient servant who spends the hours of the night prostrating and standing, wary of the Hereafter and hoping for the mercy of his Lord. Then it asks a question that awakens minds: are those who know equal to those who do not know?

أَمَّنْ هُوَ قَانِتٌ آنَاءَ اللَّيْلِ سَاجِدًا وَقَائِمًا يَحْذَرُ الْآخِرَةَ وَيَرْجُو رَحْمَةَ رَبِّهِ ۗ قُلْ هَلْ يَسْتَوِي الَّذِينَ يَعْلَمُونَ وَالَّذِينَ لَا يَعْلَمُونَ ۗ إِنَّمَا يَتَذَكَّرُ أُولُو الْأَلْبَابِ

A subtle insight in how fear and hope are distributed: wariness is attached to the Hereafter and the reckoning in it, and hope is attached to the mercy of the Lord. In attributing mercy to “his Lord” there is intimacy and nearness, as if his hope is connected to the One who nurtured him and was good to him. Then the verse makes this state a sign of true knowledge, for beneficial knowledge is that which produces reverent fear and action.

en.title: And Speak to Him a Gentle Word
en.excerpt: If gentle speech was commanded with the most tyrannical of tyrants, others are even more deserving of kindness.

body.text: Allah commands Musa and Harun (peace be upon them) to go to Pharaoh, the most tyrannical of people, and address him with soft, gentle words, in the hope that he might take heed or fear. The way of calling to good is gentleness, not harshness.
فَقُولَا لَهُ قَوْلًا لَيِّنًا لَعَلَّهُ يَتَذَكَّرُ أَوْ يَخْشَىٰ

A subtle insight in the words “that perhaps he may take heed or fear”: although Allah knew Pharaoh's state, the expression came in the form of hope, so that the caller remains attached to hope and deals with the one addressed as someone capable of being guided. Gentleness opens the door to taking heed, and harshness closes it. If this was the case with Pharaoh, how then with a parent, a spouse, a friend or a colleague?

en.title: Our Lord, You Did Not Create This in Vain; Glory Be to You
en.excerpt: Glorification comes in the middle of the supplication of the people of understanding, between reflecting on creation and asking for salvation.

body.text: Allah describes the people of understanding as those who remember Him standing, sitting and lying on their sides, and reflect on the creation of the heavens and the earth. They say that this creation was not without purpose, declare their Lord free of imperfection, and ask Him to protect them from the Fire.
الَّذِينَ يَذْكُرُونَ اللَّهَ قِيَامًا وَقُعُودًا وَعَلَىٰ جُنُوبِهِمْ وَيَتَفَكَّرُونَ فِي خَلْقِ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ رَبَّنَا مَا خَلَقْتَ هَٰذَا بَاطِلًا سُبْحَانَكَ فَقِنَا عَذَابَ النَّارِ

A subtle insight in the position of “Glory be to You”: it comes between their saying “You did not create this in vain” and their saying “so protect us from the punishment of the Fire.” Reflection led them to declare Allah's perfection, and that led them to fear and supplication. The verse also combines remembrance in every state with reflection: remembrance gives life to the heart and reflection establishes certainty. So make your contemplation of the universe an act of worship that ends in glorification and supplication.

sources: The Holy Qur'an — Surah Al Imran: 191

en.title: We Will Surely Guide Them to Our Ways
en.excerpt: He said “Our ways” in the plural: the paths of good leading to Allah are many for whoever strives against himself.

body.text: Surah Al-'Ankabut closes with an emphatic promise: those who strive against themselves seeking Allah's pleasure, He will surely guide them to the paths of guidance, and Allah is with the doers of good with help and support. It is an ending that opens the door of hope for everyone who strives toward his Lord.
وَٱلَّذِينَ جَٰهَدُواْ فِينَا لَنَهۡدِيَنَّهُمۡ سُبُلَنَاۚ وَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَمَعَ ٱلۡمُحۡسِنِينَ

A subtle insight in the words “for Us” (fina): the striving here is sincerely for Allah and in His way, not for any other aim. Then the answer comes emphasised with both lam and nun, “We will surely guide them,” to cut off any doubt about the promise, and “Our ways” comes in the plural to indicate the many and varied doors of good.

Whoever is sincere in striving against himself will have opened to him good he did not expect. He may begin with the door of prayer, and then the doors of charity, kindness and knowledge are opened to him. So take one sincere step, and Allah will guide you to what comes after it.

en.title: As It Was Prescribed for Those Before You
en.excerpt: Likening fasting to what was prescribed for earlier peoples eases its hardship and inspires friendly competition.

body.text: The verses on fasting open by calling the believers, then tell them that fasting has been prescribed for them as it was prescribed for those before them, and close with its purpose: “that you may become God-conscious.” In these few words are touches that make this worship easier for the one fasting.
يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ كُتِبَ عَلَيۡكُمُ ٱلصِّيَامُ كَمَا كُتِبَ عَلَى ٱلَّذِينَ مِن قَبۡلِكُمۡ لَعَلَّكُمۡ تَتَّقُونَ

A subtle insight in the comparison “as it was prescribed”: it mentions that earlier nations fasted too, which eases the obligation, because a hard matter becomes lighter on the soul when it is shared by all people. It also urges us not to let others be ahead of us in obedience.

And in opening the verse with the call “O you who believe” there is gentleness and honour, as if to say: by your faith you are worthy of this act of worship. Then the ending “that you may become God-conscious” shows that hunger is not a goal in itself, but a means to taqwa.

en.title: Be Mindful of Allah, Through Whom You Ask One Another, and of the Ties of Kinship
en.excerpt: Mentioning the ties of kinship right after Allah's name, in the context of taqwa, reveals how great their standing is.

body.text: Surah An-Nisa opens by reminding people of their single origin: that Allah created them from a single soul, created from it its mate, and spread from the two of them many men and women. Then it commands them to be mindful of Allah and mindful of the ties of kinship.

يَا أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ اتَّقُوا رَبَّكُمُ الَّذِي خَلَقَكُمْ مِنْ نَفْسٍ وَاحِدَةٍ وَخَلَقَ مِنْهَا زَوْجَهَا وَبَثَّ مِنْهُمَا رِجَالًا كَثِيرًا وَنِسَاءً ۚ وَاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ الَّذِي تَسَاءَلُونَ بِهِ وَالْأَرْحَامَ ۚ إِنَّ اللَّهَ كَانَ عَلَيْكُمْ رَقِيبًا

A subtle insight in joining “and the ties of kinship” to mindfulness of Allah: being wary of severing kinship is placed in the context of being wary of disobeying Allah's command, to draw attention to the fact that the right of kinship is a great right. Beginning the verse with the single origin and closing it with kinship draws a circle: we are all from one origin, and close kin are most deserving of care. And its ending, “ever Watchful over you,” reminds us that Allah sees our keeping and our severing of ties.

en.title: And the Heart of Musa's Mother Became Empty
en.excerpt: A heart empty of all but Musa, then a divine binding that steadies it: an eloquent portrayal of a mother's state.

body.text: After the mother of Musa placed her infant in the river, the Qur'an portrays the state of her heart in a few words, and shows how she almost revealed his secret out of intense longing, had Allah not made her steadfast.
وَأَصْبَحَ فُؤَادُ أُمِّ مُوسَىٰ فَارِغًا ۖ إِنْ كَادَتْ لَتُبْدِي بِهِ لَوْلَا أَنْ رَبَطْنَا عَلَىٰ قَلْبِهَا لِتَكُونَ مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ

A subtle insight in the portrayal: describing the heart as “empty” is an eloquent expression of a heart emptied of everything except the thought of her child, leaving no room in it for any other concern. The word “became” (asbaha, literally “awoke”) suggests that this state stayed with her from the very start of her day.

Then He said, “We bound her heart,” and binding is done to something one fears may slip away; as though the heart almost flew away from intense longing, so Allah tied it firm and steadied it. Thus Allah grants patience to whoever obeys Him in the hour of weakness.

en.title: “One,” then “the Eternal Refuge”
en.excerpt: Combining the indefinite and the definite at the start of Al-Ikhlas depicts Allah's uniqueness and creation's need of Him.

body.text: A short surah that introduces the Muslim to his Lord in a way pure of any blemish. It begins by affirming His oneness, then mentions His name “As-Samad,” the One to whom creation turns in its needs. Despite its brevity, it carries tremendous meanings.

قُلْ هُوَ اللَّهُ أَحَدٌ
اللَّهُ الصَّمَدُ

A subtle insight in the wording: “One” (Ahad) comes indefinite to indicate absolute uniqueness in which nothing shares. Then the Majestic Name is repeated explicitly in “Allah, the Eternal Refuge,” rather than using a pronoun, for glorification and affirmation, and “As-Samad” comes definite to convey that He alone is the One sought in all needs.

His oneness requires that none other be worshipped, and His being the Eternal Refuge requires that none other be turned to. So when you need something, turn first to As-Samad before knocking on the doors of creation. And recite it often with reflection, for it fills the heart with tawhid and tranquility.

en.title: Whoever Desires the Immediate
en.excerpt: He called this world “the immediate,” and for the Hereafter He required an effort befitting it, not a mere wish.

body.text: The two verses divide people according to what they desire: whoever desires the immediate, Allah hastens for him in it what He wills, for whom He intends; and whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it with the effort due to it while being a believer, it is they whose effort is appreciated.

مَنْ كَانَ يُرِيدُ الْعَاجِلَةَ عَجَّلْنَا لَهُ فِيهَا مَا نَشَاءُ لِمَنْ نُرِيدُ ثُمَّ جَعَلْنَا لَهُ جَهَنَّمَ يَصْلَاهَا مَذْمُومًا مَدْحُورًا
وَمَنْ أَرَادَ الْآخِرَةَ وَسَعَىٰ لَهَا سَعْيَهَا وَهُوَ مُؤْمِنٌ فَأُولَٰئِكَ كَانَ سَعْيُهُمْ مَشْكُورًا

A subtle insight in calling this world “the immediate” (al-'ajilah): a description that reveals why souls cling to it, for it is present and quick. Reflect that worldly giving is restricted by divine will, “what We will, for whom We intend,” so not everyone who wants gets all he wants. As for the Hereafter, it requires desire, “and strives for it with its due effort,” meaning the effort befitting it, and faith; and the reward is that the effort is appreciated.

en.title: And You Will Never Reach the Mountains in Height
en.excerpt: An eloquent image revealing the smallness of the arrogant before the greatness of creation.

body.text: The verse forbids walking on the earth with arrogance and conceit, then reminds the arrogant one of his reality: however hard you strike the earth with your foot, you will not tear it apart, and however tall you try to stand, you will never reach the mountains in height.
وَلَا تَمْشِ فِي الْأَرْضِ مَرَحًا ۖ إِنَّكَ لَنْ تَخْرِقَ الْأَرْضَ وَلَنْ تَبْلُغَ الْجِبَالَ طُولًا

A subtle insight in this contrast: the arrogant one strikes the ground with his feet and raises his head, so the reply addresses both directions: “you will never tear the earth” for the one who pounds the ground, and “you will never reach the mountains” for the one who stretches himself up. He is confined between an earth he cannot tear and mountains he cannot reach. It is an image that gently breaks conceit and invites humility.

en.title: Our Lord, You Have Encompassed All Things in Mercy and Knowledge
en.excerpt: The bearers of the Throne seek forgiveness for the believers, and in their praise of Allah they mention mercy before knowledge.

body.text: The verses tell that the angels who bear the Throne and those around it glorify their Lord with praise and seek forgiveness for those who believe. They ask Allah to forgive those who repent, protect them from the punishment of Hellfire, and admit them to Paradise with the righteous among their families.

الَّذِينَ يَحْمِلُونَ الْعَرْشَ وَمَنْ حَوْلَهُ يُسَبِّحُونَ بِحَمْدِ رَبِّهِمْ وَيُؤْمِنُونَ بِهِ وَيَسْتَغْفِرُونَ لِلَّذِينَ آمَنُوا رَبَّنَا وَسِعْتَ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ رَحْمَةً وَعِلْمًا فَاغْفِرْ لِلَّذِينَ تَابُوا وَاتَّبَعُوا سَبِيلَكَ وَقِهِمْ عَذَابَ الْجَحِيمِ
رَبَّنَا وَأَدْخِلْهُمْ جَنَّاتِ عَدْنٍ الَّتِي وَعَدْتَهُمْ وَمَنْ صَلَحَ مِنْ آبَائِهِمْ وَأَزْوَاجِهِمْ وَذُرِّيَّاتِهِمْ ۚ إِنَّكَ أَنْتَ الْعَزِيزُ الْحَكِيمُ

A subtle insight in the order: they said “in mercy and knowledge,” placing mercy first because the occasion is one of asking for forgiveness, so they began with what suited their need. And mentioning knowledge after it indicates that Allah knows their sins and yet His mercy encompasses them. How great it is to be prayed for without your knowing! So be among the repentant who follow Allah's way, so that these supplications include you.

en.title: Glory Be to Your Lord, the Lord of Might
en.excerpt: A surah closes with three sentences: declaring Allah's perfection, peace upon His messengers, and praise to Him.

body.text: Surah As-Saffat closes with three short verses: declaring Allah, the Lord of Might, free of what the polytheists attribute to Him; peace upon the messengers; and praise to Allah, Lord of the worlds. It is an ending that gathers the meanings of the whole surah in a few words.

سُبْحَانَ رَبِّكَ رَبِّ الْعِزَّةِ عَمَّا يَصِفُونَ
وَسَلَامٌ عَلَى الْمُرْسَلِينَ
وَالْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ

A subtle insight in the order of this ending: it begins with declaring His perfection, “Glory be to your Lord,” negating every deficiency; then follows with peace upon the messengers who conveyed tawhid; then closes with praise, which affirms every perfection. Thus negation, affirmation and gratitude to the intermediaries are brought together.

Attributing the Lord to “Might” suits the occasion of answering what the polytheists ascribed to Him: He is the Overpowering, unharmed by their words. This order is fitting for closing a gathering or a supplication: glorification, praise for the messengers, and praise to Allah.

en.title: They Will Come to You on Foot and on Every Lean Camel
en.excerpt: He said “they will come to you,” not “they will come to the House,” making the answer to the call a coming to the one who proclaimed it.

body.text: Allah commanded Ibrahim (peace be upon him) to proclaim the Hajj to people, and promised that they would come to him on foot and riding, from every distant path. His task was to call, and the reaching was upon Allah.
وَأَذِّنْ فِي النَّاسِ بِالْحَجِّ يَأْتُوكَ رِجَالًا وَعَلَىٰ كُلِّ ضَامِرٍ يَأْتِينَ مِنْ كُلِّ فَجٍّ عَمِيقٍ

A subtle insight in the words “they will come to you”: the pilgrims come to the House, but the address makes their coming an answer to Ibrahim's call, in honour of him. And it mentions “on foot” before the riders, indicating the greatness of their longing that carried them to walk.

It describes the paths as “every deep mountain pass” (fajjin 'amiq), not merely “far”; depth suggests both distance and difficulty, as though people emerge from the depths of the earth toward the House. And people have never ceased coming from every pass in answer to that call.

en.title: And He Placed Between You Affection and Mercy
en.excerpt: Affection and mercy are the two wings of marriage: one for love, the other for tenderness.

body.text: The verse counts among the signs of Allah's power and mercy that He created for man, from his own kind, a spouse in whom to find tranquility, and placed between the spouses affection and mercy. It makes all of this a subject of reflection for people of understanding.
وَمِنْ آيَاتِهِ أَنْ خَلَقَ لَكُمْ مِنْ أَنْفُسِكُمْ أَزْوَاجًا لِتَسْكُنُوا إِلَيْهَا وَجَعَلَ بَيْنَكُمْ مَوَدَّةً وَرَحْمَةً ۚ إِنَّ فِي ذَٰلِكَ لَآيَاتٍ لِقَوْمٍ يَتَفَكَّرُونَ

A subtle insight in combining “affection” and “mercy”: affection is an outward love shown in warmth and joy, and mercy is a compassion that remains when one of them weakens, falls ill or grows old; when affection fades, mercy preserves the home. The words “that you may find tranquility in them,” with the preposition ila (toward), convey inclination, reassurance and returning, as if the spouse is a refuge in which the soul takes shelter. And the word “placed” indicates that this love is a gift from Allah, preserved by gratitude.

en.title: Walking with Modesty
en.excerpt: The preposition “upon” portrays modesty as a mount on which the young woman walks.

body.text: One of the two young women returns to Musa (peace be upon him) to invite him to her father. The Qur'an describes her walk before conveying her words, then mentions what she said in a clear, concise phrase. In a single preposition of the verse is a beautiful image.

فَجَاءَتْهُ إِحْدَاهُمَا تَمْشِي عَلَى اسْتِحْيَاءٍ قَالَتْ إِنَّ أَبِي يَدْعُوكَ لِيَجْزِيَكَ أَجْرَ مَا سَقَيْتَ لَنَا ۚ فَلَمَّا جَاءَهُ وَقَصَّ عَلَيْهِ الْقَصَصَ قَالَ لَا تَخَفْ ۖ نَجَوْتَ مِنَ الْقَوْمِ الظَّالِمِينَ

A subtle insight in the preposition: it did not say “walking with modesty” using “with” (bi), but “upon modesty” ('ala istihya'), as if modesty had become a mount on which she walks, surrounding and carrying her, which more eloquently shows how deeply modesty was rooted in her. Notice too that her words were short and clear: she attributed the invitation to her father, “My father invites you,” and explained its reason, “that he may reward you for having watered for us.” Modesty appeared in both her walk and her speech, without affectation or lengthiness.

en.title: Why “Lord of the Daybreak”?
en.excerpt: Seeking refuge in the Lord of the dawn from evils carries a hidden promise that darkness will be lifted.

body.text: Surah Al-Falaq begins with a command to seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak from the evil of what He created. It is among the first things a Muslim turns to when he fears an evil, visible or hidden, and a fortress in which the believer takes shelter in his day and night.

قُلْ أَعُوذُ بِرَبِّ الْفَلَقِ
مِنْ شَرِّ مَا خَلَقَ

A subtle insight in the choice of description: al-falaq is the daybreak from which the night splits apart, so the one seeking refuge turns to the Lord who splits darkness with light. In this is a suggestion that the One able to lift the darkness of night is able to lift evils from His servant. And “what He created” comes in general terms to include every evil among created things.

So when you seek refuge with it, bring to mind that you are turning to a Lord whose world is accustomed every day to seeing its morning after its night; so do not fear what is under His authority. Recite it often, morning and evening, with a confident heart, for sincere seeking of refuge fills the heart with safety.

en.title: And Indeed, I Am the Perpetual Forgiver of Whoever Repents
en.excerpt: The intensive form Ghaffar indicates abundant forgiveness, repeated for whoever repents time after time.

body.text: In this verse Allah promises vast forgiveness to whoever combines four things: repentance from sin, faith, righteous deeds, and then steadfastness on guidance, holding firm to it until he meets his Lord.
وَإِنِّي لَغَفَّارٌ لِمَنْ تَابَ وَآمَنَ وَعَمِلَ صَالِحًا ثُمَّ اهْتَدَىٰ

A subtle insight in the words “And indeed, I am the Perpetual Forgiver”: the statement is emphasised with inna and the lam, and the attribute comes in the intensive form, so forgiveness is not a one-time thing but abundant and repeated. Then guidance is joined with the particle thumma (then), which indicates an extended span, pointing out that what is required is steadfastness and continuing on the path, not a passing repentance followed by relapse.

en.title: No Blame Will There Be upon You Today
en.excerpt: Complete pardon at the moment of power, without blame or reminders of the past.

body.text: When Yusuf (peace be upon him) met his brothers after what they had done to him, while he was in a position of strength and authority, he said to them: There is no blame upon you today. Then he prayed for their forgiveness. His pardon was the noblest of pardons.
قَالَ لَا تَثْرِيبَ عَلَيْكُمُ الْيَوْمَ ۖ يَغْفِرُ اللَّهُ لَكُمْ ۖ وَهُوَ أَرْحَمُ الرَّاحِمِينَ

A subtle insight in the word “today” in “no blame upon you today”: Yusuf chose to negate blame on the day of the meeting, the day when reproach was most expected; if blame is negated on this day, then all the more so after it. Then he did not stop at negating blame, but followed it with a prayer: “May Allah forgive you.” Complete pardon is to close the page of the past, not to reproach someone with it, and then to wish good for the one who wronged you.

en.title: When He Called His Lord in a Hidden Call
en.excerpt: Zakariyya's supplication is described as both a “call” and “hidden,” combining the warmth of longing with the courtesy of secrecy.

body.text: Surah Maryam opens with the story of Zakariyya (peace be upon him) when he called upon his Lord in secret, mentioning his weakness, his old age and his white hair, and appealing through the fact that he had never been disappointed in his supplication to his Lord.

إِذْ نَادَىٰ رَبَّهُ نِدَاءً خَفِيًّا
قَالَ رَبِّ إِنِّي وَهَنَ الْعَظْمُ مِنِّي وَاشْتَعَلَ الرَّأْسُ شَيْبًا وَلَمْ أَكُنْ بِدُعَائِكَ رَبِّ شَقِيًّا

A subtle insight in combining “called” and “hidden”: a call originally means raising the voice, but here it is hidden, indicating intense longing together with sincerity and distance from showing off. Then Zakariyya appealed through his weakness and through Allah's beautiful custom with him: “and never have I been, in my supplication to You, my Lord, unhappy.” So appeal to your Lord through your weakness and through His past kindness to you, and keep your supplication private, for it is closer to sincerity.

en.title: Signs for People Who Are Certain
en.excerpt: Three verses and three endings: for the believers, for people who are certain, for people who reason.

body.text: The verses mention the signs of Allah's power in the heavens and the earth, then in the creation of man and the creatures He disperses, then in the alternation of night and day, the sending down of rain, and the directing of the winds.

إِنَّ فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ لَآيَاتٍ لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ
وَفِي خَلْقِكُمْ وَمَا يَبُثُّ مِنْ دَابَّةٍ آيَاتٌ لِقَوْمٍ يُوقِنُونَ
وَاخْتِلَافِ اللَّيْلِ وَالنَّهَارِ وَمَا أَنْزَلَ اللَّهُ مِنَ السَّمَاءِ مِنْ رِزْقٍ فَأَحْيَا بِهِ الْأَرْضَ بَعْدَ مَوْتِهَا وَتَصْرِيفِ الرِّيَاحِ آيَاتٌ لِقَوْمٍ يَعْقِلُونَ

A subtle insight in the variety of endings: the first ends with “for the believers,” the second with “who are certain,” and the third with “who reason.” Each kind of sign addresses one aspect of the human being, and faith, certainty and reason work together in reading the universe. This variety invites you to read the signs from more than one angle.

Notice that the middle verse, which speaks of the creation of man himself, ends with certainty: reflecting on your own creation is the nearest path to certainty. So let your reflection on the universe be a mind that understands, a heart that believes, and a certainty that holds firm, then ask Allah for more.

en.title: And When We Made the House a Place of Return for Mankind
en.excerpt: Allah described the House as a mathabah: a place to which people return again and again.

body.text: This verse mentions some of the special qualities of the Sacred House: that it is a place of return for people and a place of safety, and that Allah charged Ibrahim and Isma'il to purify it for those who circle it, those who stay in devotion, and those who bow and prostrate. In the choice of its words is a beautiful precision.

وَإِذۡ جَعَلۡنَا ٱلۡبَيۡتَ مَثَابَةٗ لِّلنَّاسِ وَأَمۡنٗا وَٱتَّخِذُواْ مِن مَّقَامِ إِبۡرَٰهِـۧمَ مُصَلّٗىۖ وَعَهِدۡنَآ إِلَىٰٓ إِبۡرَٰهِـۧمَ وَإِسۡمَٰعِيلَ أَن طَهِّرَا بَيۡتِيَ لِلطَّآئِفِينَ وَٱلۡعَٰكِفِينَ وَٱلرُّكَّعِ ٱلسُّجُودِ

A subtle insight in the word mathabah: it comes from thawb, meaning return. The House is a place to which people return and never have their fill of; whenever they leave it, they long for it. The word describes the yearning of hearts, not merely a visit of bodies. In attributing the House to Allah, “My House,” is an honour for it, and in the order “those who circle, those who stay in devotion, and those who bow and prostrate” is a gradation in the states of worship around the House: from circling, to staying, to prayer.

en.title: Say: Whatever Good You Spend Is for Parents
en.excerpt: They asked what to spend, and the answer came by first naming who deserves the spending.

body.text: The Companions asked what they should spend of their wealth, and the verse made clear that whatever good they spend should be for parents, close relatives, orphans, the needy and the traveller, and closed by saying that Allah knows every good they do.

يَسۡـَٔلُونَكَ مَاذَا يُنفِقُونَۖ قُلۡ مَآ أَنفَقۡتُم مِّنۡ خَيۡرٖ فَلِلۡوَٰلِدَيۡنِ وَٱلۡأَقۡرَبِينَ وَٱلۡيَتَٰمَىٰ وَٱلۡمَسَٰكِينِ وَٱبۡنِ ٱلسَّبِيلِۗ وَمَا تَفۡعَلُواْ مِنۡ خَيۡرٖ فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ بِهِۦ عَلِيمٞ

A subtle insight in the answer: the question was about the kind of thing to spend, and the answer said “whatever good,” to include everything beneficial, then moved on to the recipients, indicating that what matters most is knowing who deserves the giving. The recipients are ordered from nearest to farthest: parents first, then close relatives, then others. So begin with your home and family, then widen the circle, and know that the end of the verse reassures you that Allah knows what you do.

en.title: What Is Your Matter?
en.excerpt: Musa's short question and the two young women's brief answer reveal chivalry and modesty.

body.text: Musa (peace be upon him) reaches the water of Madyan and sees people watering their flocks, and sees two women holding back their sheep from the water. The scene catches his attention, so he asks them about their situation, and they answer in a few words. In this short dialogue are beautiful subtleties.

وَلَمَّا وَرَدَ مَاءَ مَدْيَنَ وَجَدَ عَلَيْهِ أُمَّةً مِنَ النَّاسِ يَسْقُونَ وَوَجَدَ مِنْ دُونِهِمُ امْرَأَتَيْنِ تَذُودَانِ ۖ قَالَ مَا خَطْبُكُمَا ۖ قَالَتَا لَا نَسْقِي حَتَّىٰ يُصْدِرَ الرِّعَاءُ ۖ وَأَبُونَا شَيْخٌ كَبِيرٌ

A subtle insight in the brevity: Musa asked them in two words, “What is your matter?”, the question of one who wants to help, not of one who is curious. They answered with two sentences explaining the reason and the excuse: they do not water until the shepherds depart, and “our father is a very old man,” so he cannot do the watering. They mentioned their father's condition so it would be known that they had come out only out of need. And the phrase “apart from them” portrays them standing away from the crowd. The verse paints a complete scene of chivalry, modesty and need in a few words.

en.title: But You Do Not Understand Their Glorification
en.excerpt: Ending the verse on the universe's glorification with forbearance and forgiveness opens the door of hope for those heedless of glorifying Him.

body.text: The verse tells that the seven heavens and the earth and whoever is in them glorify Allah, and that there is nothing that does not glorify Him with praise, but human beings do not understand the glorification of these creatures. How magnificent is this cosmic scene!
تُسَبِّحُ لَهُ السَّمَاوَاتُ السَّبْعُ وَالْأَرْضُ وَمَنْ فِيهِنَّ ۚ وَإِنْ مِنْ شَيْءٍ إِلَّا يُسَبِّحُ بِحَمْدِهِ وَلَٰكِنْ لَا تَفْقَهُونَ تَسْبِيحَهُمْ ۗ إِنَّهُ كَانَ حَلِيمًا غَفُورًا

A subtle insight in the verse's ending: it could have ended with knowledge or power, but it ended with “Forbearing, Forgiving,” because the context exposes man's heedlessness: everything around him glorifies while he is heedless. So it was fitting to mention Allah's forbearance, which does not hasten punishment upon him, and His forgiveness for whoever returns to Him. This opens the door of hope for everyone who falls short.

The words “glorifies with His praise” combine declaring His perfection with praising Him, so the glorification of the universe is not a lifeless silence. When you see a tree or the sky, know that it is in worship, and be more deserving of glorification than it is. So keep regular portions of glorification in your day.

en.title: And Each of Them Will Come to Him on the Day of Resurrection Alone
en.excerpt: After mentioning the multitude of creatures and their being counted, each comes to his Lord alone, without wealth or followers.

body.text: The verses affirm that everyone in the heavens and the earth will come to the Most Merciful as a humble servant. Allah has counted them and numbered them exactly, and each of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone, accompanied by no one.

إِنْ كُلُّ مَنْ فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ إِلَّا آتِي الرَّحْمَٰنِ عَبْدًا
لَقَدْ أَحْصَاهُمْ وَعَدَّهُمْ عَدًّا
وَكُلُّهُمْ آتِيهِ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ فَرْدًا

A subtle insight in closing with “each will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection alone”: after mentioning the vast multitude of creatures and their counting and numbering, each one comes by himself, not dissolving into the crowd nor hiding among people. And in the words “will come to the Most Merciful as a servant” is an indication that all are servants of a Lord whose mercy encompasses all things. So prepare for that standing what will keep you company in your solitude.

en.title: So Overlook with Gracious Forbearance
en.excerpt: Describing forbearance as gracious means overlooking without reproach or hurt.

body.text: After reminding that Allah created the heavens and the earth in truth, and that the Hour is coming, the verse commanded overlooking the wrongdoers. Whoever is certain that the reckoning is coming finds it easy to leave his right to Allah.
وَمَا خَلَقْنَا السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضَ وَمَا بَيْنَهُمَا إِلَّا بِالْحَقِّ ۗ وَإِنَّ السَّاعَةَ لَآتِيَةٌ ۖ فَاصْفَحِ الصَّفْحَ الْجَمِيلَ

A subtle insight in describing it as “gracious forbearance” (as-safh al-jamil): not every overlooking is gracious. A person may overlook and then reproach and remind of his favour, or overlook with his tongue while rancour remains in his heart. Gracious forbearance is that which carries no reproach, no hurt and no reminders. And in mentioning the Hour before the command to overlook is a subtle link: rights are preserved with Allah.

en.title: Then Glorify the Praise of Your Lord and Seek His Forgiveness
en.excerpt: At the completion of victory and conquest, the command was not to rejoice and celebrate, but to glorify and seek forgiveness.

body.text: In Surah An-Nasr, after Allah gave His Prophet ﷺ the glad tidings of the coming of victory and conquest and people entering Allah's religion in crowds, He commanded him to glorify the praise of his Lord and seek His forgiveness, and told him that He, glory be to Him, is ever Accepting of repentance.
فَسَبِّحْ بِحَمْدِ رَبِّكَ وَاسْتَغْفِرْهُ ۚ إِنَّهُ كَانَ تَوَّابًا

A subtle insight in the position of seeking forgiveness: the command to it came at the moment of achievement, not at the moment of shortcoming, teaching the servant to seal his deeds with glorification and seeking forgiveness, because no deed is free of deficiency. And “Accepting of repentance” (Tawwab) came in the intensive form, meaning one who accepts repentance abundantly. So when you complete a task or achieve a success, praise Allah and seek His forgiveness, for this better preserves the blessing and keeps you further from self-admiration.

en.title: And That It Is He Who Makes Laugh and Makes Weep
en.excerpt: “He” was added with laughter and weeping, death and life, because people may attribute these to others.

body.text: In a context listing Allah's actions, the verses affirm that to Allah is the return and final destination of His servants, that it is He who makes laugh and makes weep, and that it is He who causes death and gives life. All these are actions connected with man's life from its beginning to its end.

وَأَنَّ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ الْمُنْتَهَىٰ
وَأَنَّهُ هُوَ أَضْحَكَ وَأَبْكَىٰ
وَأَنَّهُ هُوَ أَمَاتَ وَأَحْيَا
