A subtle insight in the pronoun “He” in “and that it is He who makes laugh and makes weep” and “and that it is He who causes death and gives life”: it conveys exclusivity and emphasis, meaning He and no other. This came with laughter and weeping, death and life, because these are matters whose outward causes a person may think are the real doers.

In combining opposites, “makes laugh and makes weep” and “causes death and gives life,” is a demonstration that all changes of state are in Allah's hand. So do not be deluded by your laughter, and do not despair in your weeping, for the One who made you weep is able to make you laugh. Return to Him in both states.

en.title: Indeed, the Hours of the Night Are More Effective
en.excerpt: Night worship is firmer in the heart, more upright in speech, and closer to presence of mind.

body.text: This verse explains the secret behind the command to pray at night in Surah Al-Muzzammil: worship that arises at night has a special quality that daytime worship does not have. What is the secret of this special quality? The answer lies in the very words of the verse.
إِنَّ نَاشِئَةَ اللَّيْلِ هِيَ أَشَدُّ وَطْئًا وَأَقْوَمُ قِيلًا

A subtle insight in the choice of nashi'ah: it is the worship that arises and is performed at night, as if rising after sleep were a new birth for the soul. Then it is described with two descriptions: “more firm in impression,” meaning heavier on the soul and firmer in effect, and “more upright in speech,” meaning more correct in recitation and closer to reflection. The two descriptions combine the meaning of striving with the meaning of its fruit: what demands greater effort yields deeper presence. In the stillness of the night, the heart and tongue are in harmony in understanding what is recited.

en.title: And Reconciliation Is Best
en.excerpt: A short, unqualified sentence affirming that reconciliation is good in every case.

body.text: The verse addresses a wife's fear of her husband's ill-conduct or turning away, and shows that there is no blame on them if they reach a settlement that preserves their home. Then it affirms that reconciliation is best.

وَإِنِ امْرَأَةٌ خَافَتْ مِنْ بَعْلِهَا نُشُوزًا أَوْ إِعْرَاضًا فَلَا جُنَاحَ عَلَيْهِمَا أَنْ يُصْلِحَا بَيْنَهُمَا صُلْحًا ۚ وَالصُّلْحُ خَيْرٌ ۗ وَأُحْضِرَتِ الْأَنْفُسُ الشُّحَّ ۚ وَإِنْ تُحْسِنُوا وَتَتَّقُوا فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ كَانَ بِمَا تَعْمَلُونَ خَبِيرًا

A subtle insight in the words “and reconciliation is best”: the sentence comes short and unqualified; it does not say “better than such-and-such,” so that it becomes a general rule suitable for every dispute. Then it says, “and souls are prone to stinginess,” as though stinginess is always present in souls, preventing them from conceding; and so it closes by urging good conduct and taqwa. If reconciliation becomes difficult, know that stinginess is standing in its way.

en.title: So Your Lord Intended
en.excerpt: The varied attribution of intention in the righteous servant's words teaches a lofty courtesy toward Allah.

body.text: The righteous servant reveals to Musa (peace be upon him) the wisdom behind what he did with the boy and the wall, showing that behind the events Musa found strange lay mercy and kindness he could not see. In the way he presents this wisdom is a fine courtesy.

فَأَرَدۡنَآ أَن يُبۡدِلَهُمَا رَبُّهُمَا خَيۡرٗا مِّنۡهُ زَكَوٰةٗ وَأَقۡرَبَ رُحۡمٗا
وَأَمَّا ٱلۡجِدَارُ فَكَانَ لِغُلَٰمَيۡنِ يَتِيمَيۡنِ فِي ٱلۡمَدِينَةِ وَكَانَ تَحۡتَهُۥ كَنزٞ لَّهُمَا وَكَانَ أَبُوهُمَا صَٰلِحٗا فَأَرَادَ رَبُّكَ أَن يَبۡلُغَآ أَشُدَّهُمَا وَيَسۡتَخۡرِجَا كَنزَهُمَا رَحۡمَةٗ مِّن رَّبِّكَۚ وَمَا فَعَلۡتُهُۥ عَنۡ أَمۡرِيۚ ذَٰلِكَ تَأۡوِيلُ مَا لَمۡ تَسۡطِع عَّلَيۡهِ صَبۡرٗا

A subtle insight in how intention is attributed: concerning the boy he said “so we intended,” and concerning the wall, in which there was pure good for the two young orphans, he said “so your Lord intended,” and then “as a mercy from your Lord.” He attributed pure good to Allah alone, out of courtesy and reverence. And in the words “and their father had been righteous” is a subtle indication that the righteousness of parents extends its effect to their children through Allah's protection of them. Whoever wants good for his offspring should begin by reforming himself.

en.title: If We Willed, We Could Make It Bitter
en.excerpt: Dropping the emphatic lam in the verse about water, but not in the verse about crops, is a meaningful rhetorical subtlety.

body.text: The verses ask man about the fresh water he drinks: is it you who brought it down from the clouds, or is Allah the One who sends it down? If He willed, He could make it intensely salty and undrinkable; so why are you not grateful?

أَفَرَءَيْتُمُ ٱلْمَآءَ ٱلَّذِى تَشْرَبُونَ
ءَأَنتُمْ أَنزَلْتُمُوهُ مِنَ ٱلْمُزْنِ أَمْ نَحْنُ ٱلْمُنزِلُونَ
لَوْ نَشَآءُ جَعَلْنَٰهُ أُجَاجًۭا فَلَوْلَا تَشْكُرُونَ

A subtle insight in the construction: the result of the condition here, “We could make it bitter,” comes without the lam, whereas in the verses about crops before it, it comes emphasised with the lam. One explanation is that a person might imagine that ruining crops is in his hand or due to earthly causes, so emphasis was needed; but as for water coming down from the clouds, no one claims to control it.

Then the verses close with “so why are you not grateful?” The fresh water that reaches us without any effort on our part in sending it down is a blessing deserving of praise. Every sip of fresh water is a silent invitation to gratitude, and a reminder not to waste it or take it lightly.

en.title: But You Prefer the Worldly Life
en.excerpt: The expression “prefer” shows that the blame is for putting this world first, not merely for living in it.

body.text: The two verses reproach those who put the worldly life first and favour it over the Hereafter, even though the Hereafter is better and more lasting: better in its bliss and purity, and more lasting in its permanence, for its bliss never ends or fades.

بَلْ تُؤْثِرُونَ ٱلْحَيَوٰةَ ٱلدُّنْيَا
وَٱلْءَاخِرَةُ خَيْرٌۭ وَأَبْقَىٰٓ

A subtle insight in the expression of preference: He did not say “but you love the world” or “you live in it,” but “but you prefer the worldly life,” and preference (ithar) is putting one thing before another when weighing them. So the blame is for giving it priority, not for benefiting from it. Then the two descriptions “better and more lasting” come together, because a thing may be good but not last, or last but not be good, and the Hereafter combines both perfections.

en.title: Even If It Be Against Yourselves
en.excerpt: True justice begins with bearing witness against oneself before one's closest relatives.

body.text: The verse commands the believers to stand firmly for justice, witnesses for Allah in truth, even if the testimony is against themselves, their parents or their relatives, whether the one testified against is rich or poor. Justice shows favour to no one.

يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا كُونُوا قَوَّامِينَ بِالْقِسْطِ شُهَدَاءَ لِلَّهِ وَلَوْ عَلَىٰ أَنْفُسِكُمْ أَوِ الْوَالِدَيْنِ وَالْأَقْرَبِينَ ۚ إِنْ يَكُنْ غَنِيًّا أَوْ فَقِيرًا فَاللَّهُ أَوْلَىٰ بِهِمَا ۖ فَلَا تَتَّبِعُوا الْهَوَىٰ أَنْ تَعْدِلُوا ۚ وَإِنْ تَلْوُوا أَوْ تُعْرِضُوا فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ كَانَ بِمَا تَعْمَلُونَ خَبِيرًا

A subtle insight in the order: the verse begins with “against yourselves,” then parents, then relatives, placing the hardest testimony, against oneself, first, because whoever is just with himself will be even more just with others. And the words “be persistently standing firm in justice” come in the intensive form to indicate permanence and abundance, not justice on a single occasion. So admit your mistake if you err, for that is the beginning of justice.

en.title: Each Has Known Its Prayer and Its Glorification
en.excerpt: The image of birds with wings outspread in the sky is a scene of glorification, and every creature knows the worship befitting it.

body.text: The verse draws attention to the fact that everyone in the heavens and the earth glorifies Allah, singling out the birds with wings outspread in the air. Then it tells that every creature has known its prayer and its glorification, and Allah knows what they do.
أَلَمْ تَرَ أَنَّ اللَّهَ يُسَبِّحُ لَهُ مَنْ فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ وَالطَّيْرُ صَافَّاتٍ ۖ كُلٌّ قَدْ عَلِمَ صَلَاتَهُ وَتَسْبِيحَهُ ۗ وَاللَّهُ عَلِيمٌ بِمَا يَفْعَلُونَ

A subtle insight in singling out “and the birds with wings outspread”: the birds are mentioned after the general statement even though they are included in it, because their state in the sky is a visible sign everyone sees, held between heaven and earth by Allah's power. Then He said “each has known,” giving every creature a prayer and a glorification that it knows, and closed with Allah's knowledge of what they do. If the birds know their glorification, man is more deserving of knowing his remembrance and keeping it up.

en.title: And He Is the Forgiving, the Loving
en.excerpt: He joined forgiveness with love: He forgives His repentant servant and then loves him.

body.text: After the surah mentioned the severity of Allah's grip on the wrongdoers, these verses came: He is the Forgiving of the sins of those who repent, the Loving who loves His allies, Owner of the glorious Throne, Doer of whatever He intends. Thus the mention of mercy comes together with the mention of majesty.

وَهُوَ الْغَفُورُ الْوَدُودُ
ذُو الْعَرْشِ الْمَجِيدُ
فَعَّالٌ لِمَا يُرِيدُ

A subtle insight in joining “the Forgiving” with “the Loving”: forgiveness is the erasing of sin, and love comes after it. The one who repents does not merely have his sin covered; his Lord turns to him with love. And this came after the mention of His severe grip, so that fear and hope come together in the servant's heart.

Then it closes with “Doer of whatever He intends,” in the intensive form: nothing stands between Him and what He wills. If He wills to forgive you and love you, nothing can prevent it. So turn to Him in repentance, however many your sins, and think well of Him.

en.title: And Indeed, It Is Difficult Except for the Humbly Submissive
en.excerpt: Prayer is heavy for many people, but light for the people of humility.

body.text: The verse commands seeking help through patience and prayer in the affairs of life, then acknowledges that this is heavy on souls, except for the humbly submissive who are certain that they will meet their Lord. In the wording of the two verses is a precision worth pausing over.

وَٱسۡتَعِينُواْ بِٱلصَّبۡرِ وَٱلصَّلَوٰةِۚ وَإِنَّهَا لَكَبِيرَةٌ إِلَّا عَلَى ٱلۡخَٰشِعِينَ
ٱلَّذِينَ يَظُنُّونَ أَنَّهُم مُّلَٰقُواْ رَبِّهِمۡ وَأَنَّهُمۡ إِلَيۡهِ رَٰجِعُونَ

A subtle insight in the words “who think that they will meet their Lord”: “think” (zann) here means certainty, and the expression was used to show that merely bringing the meeting to mind is enough to make worship lighter; how much more for one who is certain of it? This reflects the breadth of Arabic in using zann to mean knowledge. And in the exception “except for the humbly submissive” is a demonstration that the heaviness of worship is not in the worship itself but in the state of the heart; when the heart is humble, what was heavy becomes light, and indeed becomes a delight and a source of comfort.

en.title: After Satan Had Sown Discord Between Me and My Brothers
en.excerpt: Yusuf attributed the rift to Satan's sowing of discord, to protect the feelings of his brothers standing before him.

body.text: In the scene of Yusuf's reunion with his parents and brothers, he raised his parents onto the throne and remembered Allah's kindness to him when He brought him out of prison and brought his family from the desert, after Satan had sown discord between him and his brothers.

وَرَفَعَ أَبَوَيْهِ عَلَى الْعَرْشِ وَخَرُّوا لَهُ سُجَّدًا ۖ وَقَالَ يَا أَبَتِ هَٰذَا تَأْوِيلُ رُؤْيَايَ مِنْ قَبْلُ قَدْ جَعَلَهَا رَبِّي حَقًّا ۖ وَقَدْ أَحْسَنَ بِي إِذْ أَخْرَجَنِي مِنَ السِّجْنِ وَجَاءَ بِكُمْ مِنَ الْبَدْوِ مِنْ بَعْدِ أَنْ نَزَغَ الشَّيْطَانُ بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَ إِخْوَتِي ۚ إِنَّ رَبِّي لَطِيفٌ لِمَا يَشَاءُ ۚ إِنَّهُ هُوَ الْعَلِيمُ الْحَكِيمُ

A subtle insight in the words “He brought me out of prison”: he did not mention the well into which his brothers threw him, even though it was harsher, to protect their feelings and out of generosity in pardon. And in the words “between me and my brothers” he made the dispute one between two parties; he did not say Satan incited my brothers, so he did not lay the responsibility on them alone. This is how to speak about past disputes: without wounding and without reopening wounds.

en.title: And Let Him Be Gentle
en.excerpt: A single word in the young men's instructions combines caution and good conduct.

body.text: The People of the Cave wake after a long sleep and ask one another how long they have remained. Then they move from argument to what benefits them, sending one of them to buy them food and giving him precise instructions.

وَكَذَٰلِكَ بَعَثۡنَٰهُمۡ لِيَتَسَآءَلُواْ بَيۡنَهُمۡۚ قَالَ قَآئِلٞ مِّنۡهُمۡ كَمۡ لَبِثۡتُمۡۖ قَالُواْ لَبِثۡنَا يَوۡمًا أَوۡ بَعۡضَ يَوۡمٖۚ قَالُواْ رَبُّكُمۡ أَعۡلَمُ بِمَا لَبِثۡتُمۡ فَٱبۡعَثُوٓاْ أَحَدَكُم بِوَرِقِكُمۡ هَٰذِهِۦٓ إِلَى ٱلۡمَدِينَةِ فَلۡيَنظُرۡ أَيُّهَآ أَزۡكَىٰ طَعَامٗا فَلۡيَأۡتِكُم بِرِزۡقٖ مِّنۡهُ وَلۡيَتَلَطَّفۡ وَلَا يُشۡعِرَنَّ بِكُمۡ أَحَدًا

A subtle insight in the transition: when they differed about how long they had stayed, they said, “Your Lord knows best how long you have remained,” cutting off a pointless debate and occupying themselves with what they actually needed. This is a courtesy in leaving discussion that bears no fruit in action. Then they instructed their companion to look for “whichever has the purest food,” not content with just any food but seeking the best and purest, and to “be gentle,” meaning to act with kindness and caution. The instruction combined wholesome earnings with good conduct.

en.title: Allah Will Bring About Ease After Hardship
en.excerpt: The near-future “will” and the indefinite “hardship” and “ease” carry glad tidings for everyone whose provision is tight.

body.text: The verse comes in the context of maintenance: let the one with abundance spend from his abundance, and let the one whose provision is restricted spend from what Allah has given him, for Allah does not burden a soul beyond what He has given it. Then it closes with a promise that reassures the weak.
لِيُنْفِقْ ذُو سَعَةٍ مِنْ سَعَتِهِ ۖ وَمَنْ قُدِرَ عَلَيْهِ رِزْقُهُ فَلْيُنْفِقْ مِمَّا آتَاهُ اللَّهُ ۚ لَا يُكَلِّفُ اللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا مَا آتَاهَا ۚ سَيَجْعَلُ اللَّهُ بَعْدَ عُسْرٍ يُسْرًا

A subtle insight in the words “Allah will bring about” (sa-yaj'alu): the prefix sa indicates the near future, as though ease is certainly coming, and its coming expressed by the verb “bring about,” attributed to Allah, makes it a promise from the All-Powerful who never breaks His word. And “hardship” and “ease” come indefinite, so whatever hardship it may be, after it comes an ease that suits it.

This promise coming after the words “Allah does not burden a soul” is a consolation for the one whose wealth is little: he is not required to give what he does not have, and he awaits near relief from his Lord. So be patient, trusting in His promise, for His promise is true.

en.title: As Though They Had Remained Only an Hour
en.excerpt: A long lifetime shrinks on the Day of Gathering until it seems an hour of a day.

body.text: The verse depicts the Day of Gathering: Allah gathers people, and they feel as though they had stayed in the world only an hour of the day, recognising one another. Those who denied the meeting with Allah have lost, and they were not guided.
وَيَوْمَ يَحْشُرُهُمْ كَأَنْ لَمْ يَلْبَثُوا إِلَّا سَاعَةً مِنَ النَّهَارِ يَتَعَارَفُونَ بَيْنَهُمْ ۚ قَدْ خَسِرَ الَّذِينَ كَذَّبُوا بِلِقَاءِ اللَّهِ وَمَا كَانُوا مُهْتَدِينَ

A subtle insight in the words “an hour of the day”: it does not stop at mentioning an hour, but specifies it as an hour of the day, and an hour of the day passes amid busyness without being noticed, which makes the sense of brevity even greater. This is how entire lifetimes will seem on that Day. And in the words “recognising one another” is an indication that those whose company we kept will be present; so let your companionship be of the kind that benefits you on that Day.

en.title: And Enjoined One Another to Compassion
en.excerpt: The form “enjoined one another” makes patience and compassion a mutual responsibility among the believers.

body.text: Among the qualities of the people of good who attempted the steep path, the verse mentions that they believed, enjoined one another to patience, and enjoined one another to compassion. An individual's righteousness is not complete without contributing to the righteousness of others.
ثُمَّ كَانَ مِنَ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَتَوَاصَوْا بِالصَّبْرِ وَتَوَاصَوْا بِالْمَرْحَمَةِ

A subtle insight in the form “and enjoined one another to compassion” (tawasaw), on the pattern of reciprocity: it indicates mutual participation, meaning each of them advises others and accepts advice from them, so no one is above advice. The verb is repeated with both patience and compassion to stress that each is an independent virtue deserving to be mutually enjoined. So be one who enjoins compassion, and one who accepts being enjoined to it.

en.title: We Hear and We Obey; Your Forgiveness, Our Lord
en.excerpt: Directly after declaring that they hear and obey, the believers asked for forgiveness, not deluded by their obedience.

body.text: The verse describes the faith of the Messenger ﷺ and the believers in Allah, His angels, His books and His messengers, without distinguishing between any of them; their declaration that they hear and obey; then their request for forgiveness and their acknowledgment that the final return is to Allah.

ءَامَنَ ٱلرَّسُولُ بِمَآ أُنزِلَ إِلَيۡهِ مِن رَّبِّهِۦ وَٱلۡمُؤۡمِنُونَۚ كُلٌّ ءَامَنَ بِٱللَّهِ وَمَلَٰٓئِكَتِهِۦ وَكُتُبِهِۦ وَرُسُلِهِۦ لَا نُفَرِّقُ بَيۡنَ أَحَدٖ مِّن رُّسُلِهِۦۚ وَقَالُواْ سَمِعۡنَا وَأَطَعۡنَاۖ غُفۡرَانَكَ رَبَّنَا وَإِلَيۡكَ ٱلۡمَصِيرُ

A subtle insight in the connection: they said “we hear and we obey” and immediately followed it with “Your forgiveness, our Lord,” for obedience, however complete, is not free of shortcomings that need forgiveness. And “Your forgiveness” (ghufranaka) comes as a verbal noun in the accusative, like an insistent request, meaning: we ask You for Your forgiveness. So whenever you obey Allah, do not look at your deed with admiration; rather, close it by asking for forgiveness.

en.title: Except That Upon Allah Is Its Provision
en.excerpt: He said “upon Allah,” a form expressing commitment: Allah has guaranteed the provision of every creature out of His grace.

body.text: The verse affirms that there is no creature moving on the earth except that Allah has guaranteed its provision. He knows its place of dwelling and its place of deposit, and all of that is in a clear record. Nothing of its affairs is hidden from Him.
وَمَا مِنْ دَابَّةٍ فِي الْأَرْضِ إِلَّا عَلَى اللَّهِ رِزْقُهَا وَيَعْلَمُ مُسْتَقَرَّهَا وَمُسْتَوْدَعَهَا ۚ كُلٌّ فِي كِتَابٍ مُبِينٍ

A subtle insight in the expression “upon Allah is its provision”: the preposition “upon” ('ala) indicates commitment, as though Allah has made the provision of His creatures a right He has committed Himself to out of grace and generosity, not an obligation imposed on Him by another. And the negation followed by exception, “there is no creature... except,” includes every creature without exception.

Then He joined provision with knowledge: “and He knows its place of dwelling and place of deposit.” The One who guarantees provision knows where its owner is and where he will end up, so no one is lost to Him. So be reassured by this promise, and strive to seek the lawful with a calm heart.

en.title: Certainly Will the Believers Have Succeeded
en.excerpt: Opening the surah with qad and the past tense makes the believers' success a certainty.

body.text: Surah Al-Mu'minun begins by announcing the success of the believers, then mentions the first of their qualities: that they are humble in their prayer. Humility was the first thing they were described with. In every word of these two verses is a beautiful touch.

قَدْ أَفْلَحَ ٱلْمُؤْمِنُونَ
ٱلَّذِينَ هُمْ فِى صَلَاتِهِمْ خَٰشِعُونَ

A subtle insight in the words “certainly succeeded” (qad aflaha): qad with the past tense conveys certainty, as though their success has already happened and been completed, even though the reward is in the future; this expresses the certainty of the promise. Then He said “in their prayer” rather than “they pray,” making the prayer a space that contains them, and humility a state that fills them within it. Notice that these qualities begin with prayer and, a few verses later, end with guarding it; so prayer is like a wall surrounding all the other virtues: the believer's qualities begin with it and end with it.

en.title: And Give the Relative His Right
en.excerpt: Allah called what is given to a relative a “right,” not a favour or a kindness.

body.text: The verse commands giving the relative his right, and giving to the needy and the traveller cut off from his family and wealth. Then it forbids extravagance and spending wealth where it does not belong. It thus combines generosity in rights with wisdom in spending.
وَآتِ ذَا الْقُرْبَىٰ حَقَّهُ وَالْمِسْكِينَ وَابْنَ السَّبِيلِ وَلَا تُبَذِّرْ تَبْذِيرًا

A subtle insight in the words “his right”: the right is attributed to the relative, as though he has a fixed share in your wealth, and when you give to him you are fulfilling your duty, not doing him a favour. This preserves the dignity of the receiver and purifies the giver of reminding others of his favours. The prohibition of extravagance comes after the command to give, so that the balance is clear: wealth is spent on rights before luxuries. So review your spending, and set a known share for your kin.

en.title: What Allah Wills; There Is No Power Except with Allah
en.excerpt: A phrase said on seeing a blessing moves the heart from self-admiration to acknowledging Allah's favour.

body.text: In the story of the owner of the two gardens, the believing man advises his companion who was deluded by his wealth, and points him to the words he should have said when he entered his garden and saw the good in it.
وَلَوۡلَآ إِذۡ دَخَلۡتَ جَنَّتَكَ قُلۡتَ مَا شَآءَ ٱللَّهُ لَا قُوَّةَ إِلَّا بِٱللَّهِۚ إِن تَرَنِ أَنَا۠ أَقَلَّ مِنكَ مَالٗا وَوَلَدٗا

A subtle insight in the timing: the phrase is tied to the moment “when you entered your garden,” that is, immediately on seeing the blessing, because that is the moment when pride creeps into the heart. So “ma sha' Allah” (what Allah wills) comes to return the favour to its true Owner.

The phrase combines affirming the will of Allah, “what Allah wills,” with negating power from any other, “there is no power except with Allah.” Whoever says it upon seeing his blessings in his home, wealth and children protects his heart from self-admiration, and remembers that what he has is a gift that may be taken back.

en.title: My Lord Has Honoured Me... My Lord Has Humiliated Me
en.excerpt: The two verses correct man's scale: abundance and constraint are both tests, not signs of honour or disgrace.

body.text: The two verses describe man's nature when his Lord tests him: if He honours him and grants him favour, he thinks it is proof of his honour with Allah; and if He restricts his provision, he thinks it is proof of his disgrace before Him.

فَأَمَّا الْإِنْسَانُ إِذَا مَا ابْتَلَاهُ رَبُّهُ فَأَكْرَمَهُ وَنَعَّمَهُ فَيَقُولُ رَبِّي أَكْرَمَنِ
وَأَمَّا إِذَا مَا ابْتَلَاهُ فَقَدَرَ عَلَيْهِ رِزْقَهُ فَيَقُولُ رَبِّي أَهَانَنِ

A subtle insight in the wording: the word “tests him” comes in both cases, so honouring with blessing is a test, and restriction of provision is a test. Notice that in the case of abundance the verse said “and honours him and favours him,” attributing the honour to Allah, while in the case of constraint it said “and restricts his provision” and did not say “and humiliates him”; humiliation is man's assumption, not the reality of what his Lord did.

So do not make the abundance or scarcity of wealth a measure of your standing with Allah; rather, look at your state in each: were you grateful in abundance, and were you patient in constraint? That is the real test. So ask Allah for gratitude and patience together.

en.title: So Let Not the Worldly Life Delude You
en.excerpt: The verse warns against two delusions: the world with its adornment, and Satan with his false hopes.

body.text: The verse calls all people, affirming that Allah's promise of resurrection and recompense is true beyond doubt. Then it warns them of two things: that the worldly life deceive them with its pleasures, and that the Deceiver, Satan, deceive them concerning Allah.
يَا أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ إِنَّ وَعْدَ اللَّهِ حَقٌّ ۖ فَلَا تَغُرَّنَّكُمُ الْحَيَاةُ الدُّنْيَا ۖ وَلَا يَغُرَّنَّكُمْ بِاللَّهِ الْغَرُورُ

A subtle insight in the verse's structure: it begins by establishing the truth, “Indeed, the promise of Allah is true,” and then derives the prohibition from it, for knowledge of the promise is the fortress against deception. The prohibition comes emphasised with the nun twice: once against the delusion of the world with its glitter, and once against Satan who deludes concerning Allah, making sin seem trivial and arousing hope of forgiveness without repentance.

en.title: A Good Word Is Like a Good Tree
en.excerpt: A good word is like a tree: a firm root, a lofty branch, and lasting fruit.

body.text: The verse strikes a parable of a good word as a good tree, whose root is firm in the ground and whose branches rise high in the sky. It brings the meaning close to minds through a living image that people see in their lives every day and benefit from.
أَلَمْ تَرَ كَيْفَ ضَرَبَ اللَّهُ مَثَلًا كَلِمَةً طَيِّبَةً كَشَجَرَةٍ طَيِّبَةٍ أَصْلُهَا ثَابِتٌ وَفَرْعُهَا فِي السَّمَاءِ

A subtle insight in the use of the parable: a tree does not bear fruit in a single day; it needs a deep root and time. Likewise, the effect of a good word extends and accumulates. And in combining “its root is firm” with “its branches are in the sky” is an indication that a good word is sincere in its inner reality and lofty in its effect. So choose your words carefully, for with them you may plant a tree under whose shade others rest for years.

en.title: My Lord, Forgive and Have Mercy, and You Are the Best of the Merciful
en.excerpt: A short supplication with its object omitted, so it widens to include every sin and every mercy.

body.text: Surah Al-Mu'minun closes with this short, comprehensive supplication, in which Allah commands His Prophet ﷺ to ask Him for forgiveness and mercy, appealing to Him as the best of those who show mercy, after the surah mentioned the qualities of the believers and the fate of the heedless.
وَقُل رَّبِّ ٱغْفِرْ وَٱرْحَمْ وَأَنتَ خَيْرُ ٱلرَّٰحِمِينَ

A subtle insight in the omission: no specific sin or type of mercy is mentioned; the two verbs come without an object, “forgive and have mercy,” so the request includes every sin, everyone shown mercy, and every kind of mercy. Then it closes with “the best of the merciful,” because Allah's mercy is above the mercy of every merciful one. So memorise this comprehensive supplication, and repeat it in your prostration and at the end of your day.

en.title: There Is Nothing Like Him, and He Is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing
en.excerpt: The verse combines negating likeness and affirming attributes in a single balanced sentence.

body.text: The verse mentions that Allah is the Originator of the heavens and the earth, who made for people mates from among themselves and from the livestock mates, then affirms that there is nothing like Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing. It is among the most comprehensive verses on making Allah known.
فَاطِرُ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ ۚ جَعَلَ لَكُمْ مِنْ أَنْفُسِكُمْ أَزْوَاجًا وَمِنَ الْأَنْعَامِ أَزْوَاجًا ۖ يَذْرَؤُكُمْ فِيهِ ۚ لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِ شَيْءٌ ۖ وَهُوَ السَّمِيعُ الْبَصِيرُ

A subtle insight in the composition of this sentence: it begins with negation, “there is nothing like Him,” declaring Allah free of resemblance to His creation, then follows with affirmation, “and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing,” affirming for Him attributes of perfection. Thus declaring Him free of imperfection does not mean denying His attributes, nor does affirming them mean likening Him to creation.

Its coming after the mention of mates is subtle: all created things were made in pairs that resemble one another, while Allah alone has no like. And in closing with the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing is reassurance for the one who supplicates: your Lord, whom nothing resembles, hears you and sees you. So call upon Him with confidence.

en.title: By Night and by Day, Secretly and Publicly
en.excerpt: In describing those who spend, He mentioned night before day, and secret before public.

body.text: The verse describes those who spend their wealth at all times and in all states, by night and by day, secretly and publicly, and promises them reward and safety from fear and grief. In the order of its words is a subtle secret worth reflecting on.
ٱلَّذِينَ يُنفِقُونَ أَمۡوَٰلَهُم بِٱلَّيۡلِ وَٱلنَّهَارِ سِرّٗا وَعَلَانِيَةٗ فَلَهُمۡ أَجۡرُهُمۡ عِندَ رَبِّهِمۡ وَلَا خَوۡفٌ عَلَيۡهِمۡ وَلَا هُمۡ يَحۡزَنُونَ

A subtle insight in the order: it mentions night before day, and secret before public, because charity at night and in secret is further from showing off and closer to sincerity, so it deserved to come first. Yet it did not neglect the day and the public, for each has its place. And in covering all times and states is an indication that giving for these people is not a passing season, but a permanent trait: they spend whenever a need arises, without waiting for an occasion or an audience.

en.title: And Dutiful to His Parents, and Not a Disobedient Tyrant
en.excerpt: Yahya's dutifulness to his parents was paired with the negation of tyranny: the dutiful are not arrogant.

body.text: The verses praise Yahya (peace be upon him) for noble qualities he had from a young age, among them that he was dutiful to his parents and good to them, and was neither arrogant toward people nor disobedient to his Lord.
وَبَرًّا بِوَالِدَيْهِ وَلَمْ يَكُنْ جَبَّارًا عَصِيًّا

A subtle insight in the contrast: it mentions dutifulness and then immediately negates its opposite, “a disobedient tyrant,” because undutifulness often springs from arrogance in the soul; whoever humbles himself before his parents has broken his own tyranny. And choosing the form barr, an intensive form, indicates that dutifulness had become a firmly rooted trait in him, not a passing act. So let your dutifulness be a daily habit, not a seasonal occasion.

en.title: What My Lord Has Established Me In Is Better
en.excerpt: Dhul-Qarnayn refused payment and asked for help through work, making the people partners in the building.

body.text: A people offer Dhul-Qarnayn wealth in return for building a barrier to protect them, and he answers them with words that combine integrity and good leadership. In this answer is a subtlety in good manners and sound management.
قَالَ مَا مَكَّنِّي فِيهِ رَبِّي خَيۡرٞ فَأَعِينُونِي بِقُوَّةٍ أَجۡعَلۡ بَيۡنَكُمۡ وَبَيۡنَهُمۡ رَدۡمًا

A subtle insight in the answer: he refused the money, saying, “What my Lord has established me in is better,” attributing what he had to Allah and seeing it as sufficient for him. Then he said, “So help me with strength.” He did not reject their offer curtly, but turned their wish to help into participation in the work. In this is wisdom in leadership: that people share in building what benefits them, so they feel its value and preserve it. The strong and sincere person does not exploit people's need, but serves them with what Allah has given him.

en.title: None Can Withhold It
en.excerpt: He said “it” (feminine) for mercy and “it” (general) for what is withheld, so that mercy remains present in both cases.

body.text: The verse affirms that whatever mercy, provision and guidance Allah opens for people, no one can withhold it, and whatever He withholds, no one can release it after Him, and He is the Almighty, the All-Wise. All the keys are in His hand.
مَا يَفْتَحِ اللَّهُ لِلنَّاسِ مِنْ رَحْمَةٍ فَلَا مُمْسِكَ لَهَا ۖ وَمَا يُمْسِكْ فَلَا مُرْسِلَ لَهُ مِنْ بَعْدِهِ ۚ وَهُوَ الْعَزِيزُ الْحَكِيمُ

A subtle insight in the two pronouns: concerning opening, He said “none can withhold it” (la mumsika laha), with the pronoun referring explicitly to mercy; and concerning withholding, He said “none can release it” (la mursila lahu), with the pronoun referring to the general word “whatever.” So mercy is named explicitly at the giving, while withholding comes in general terms covering everything withheld.

Putting opening before withholding gives precedence to mercy, and ending the verse with “the Almighty, the All-Wise” makes withholding a matter of wisdom, not stinginess. So if a door is closed to you, know that all the keys of mercy are in the hand of the All-Wise.

en.title: We Will Surely Turn You to a Qiblah That Will Please You
en.excerpt: He said “that will please you,” not “that pleases Us,” honouring the Prophet ﷺ and answering what was in his heart.

body.text: This verse depicts the scene of the Prophet ﷺ turning his face toward the sky, awaiting his Lord's command regarding the qiblah. The answer comes, directing him toward the Sacred Mosque, and the believers are commanded to turn their faces toward it wherever they are.

قَدۡ نَرَىٰ تَقَلُّبَ وَجۡهِكَ فِي ٱلسَّمَآءِۖ فَلَنُوَلِّيَنَّكَ قِبۡلَةٗ تَرۡضَىٰهَاۚ فَوَلِّ وَجۡهَكَ شَطۡرَ ٱلۡمَسۡجِدِ ٱلۡحَرَامِۚ وَحَيۡثُ مَا كُنتُمۡ فَوَلُّواْ وُجُوهَكُمۡ شَطۡرَهُۥۗ وَإِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ أُوتُواْ ٱلۡكِتَٰبَ لَيَعۡلَمُونَ أَنَّهُ ٱلۡحَقُّ مِن رَّبِّهِمۡۗ وَمَا ٱللَّهُ بِغَٰفِلٍ عَمَّا يَعۡمَلُونَ

A subtle insight in the words “We have certainly seen”: the present-tense verb (nara) portrays the scene as present and recurring, and conveys that Allah sees His servant's longing and knows what is in his heart before he asks. Then the answer comes emphasised with the lam of oath and the emphatic nun in “We will surely turn you,” and described as a qiblah “that will please you.” Allah does not give His servant only what he needs, but what pleases his heart. In this is comfort for every worshipper who turns toward the qiblah.

en.title: O Son of My Mother
en.excerpt: Harun called his brother by their relation through their mother, because mentioning her is gentler and more likely to soften the heart.

body.text: When Musa returned to his people and found that they had worshipped the calf, he seized his brother Harun by his beard and head, angry for the sake of Allah. Harun addressed him, explaining his excuse: that he feared being accused of dividing the Children of Israel.
قَالَ يَا ابْنَ أُمَّ لَا تَأْخُذْ بِلِحْيَتِي وَلَا بِرَأْسِي ۖ إِنِّي خَشِيتُ أَنْ تَقُولَ فَرَّقْتَ بَيْنَ بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ وَلَمْ تَرْقُبْ قَوْلِي

A subtle insight in the words “O son of my mother”: they were brothers through both father and mother, but Harun chose to refer to their mother, because mentioning the mother evokes mercy and tenderness and recalls the shared womb, and so anger softens. In this is a courtesy for disagreements between siblings: address your brother with what stirs affection in his heart, and explain your excuse calmly rather than meeting harshness with harshness.

en.title: Be Coolness and Safety
en.excerpt: Coolness was paired with safety, so the fire became a coolness that does no harm.

body.text: Ibrahim (peace be upon him) is thrown into the fire as punishment for his belief in Allah's oneness, and the divine command comes to the fire directly, and it is transformed from its nature by the command of its Creator. In the words of this brief command is a wondrous rhetorical precision worth pausing over.
قُلۡنَا يَٰنَارُ كُونِي بَرۡدٗا وَسَلَٰمًا عَلَىٰٓ إِبۡرَٰهِيمَ

A subtle insight in the combination: the command was not limited to “coolness,” but was paired with “and safety,” because intense cold can harm just as heat harms, so safety came to make it a coolness without harm. This is among the precisions of Qur'anic expression. And the call is addressed to the fire directly, as though it hears and obeys, so that you know all causes are subject to Allah's command, and He nullifies their effect when He wills. Whoever truly relies on Allah does not fear what people threaten him with.

en.title: And Rely upon the Ever-Living Who Does Not Die
en.excerpt: For reliance He chose the description “the Ever-Living who does not die,” for every other support passes away.

body.text: Allah commands His Prophet to rely in all his affairs upon the Ever-Living, the Everlasting who does not die, and to glorify Him with praise, and sufficient is He as All-Aware of His servants' sins. It is a general command that includes every believer in every matter.
وَتَوَكَّلۡ عَلَى ٱلۡحَيِّ ٱلَّذِي لَا يَمُوتُ وَسَبِّحۡ بِحَمۡدِهِۦۚ وَكَفَىٰ بِهِۦ بِذُنُوبِ عِبَادِهِۦ خَبِيرًا

A subtle insight in choosing the description fitting the occasion: He did not mention the name alone here, but described Him as “the Ever-Living who does not die,” because reliance is dependence, and depending on one who dies or changes is deficient dependence, whereas the support of the Ever-Living, the Everlasting, is never cut off.

Then He joined reliance with glorification: “and glorify Him with praise.” The heart that relies on Allah needs nourishment from remembrance to keep it steady. So if you fear losing support from people, remember that your true support is Ever-Living and never dies. So depend on Him alone.

en.title: And They Fall upon Their Faces Weeping
en.excerpt: Repeating “they fall upon their faces” depicts a prostration renewed whenever the Qur'an's effect on the heart is renewed.

body.text: These verses describe the state of those given knowledge when the Qur'an is recited to them: they prostrate, glorify their Lord, then prostrate again weeping, and the Qur'an increases them in humility. It is a living picture of the effect of recitation on knowing hearts.

قُلْ آمِنُوا بِهِ أَوْ لَا تُؤْمِنُوا ۚ إِنَّ الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الْعِلْمَ مِنْ قَبْلِهِ إِذَا يُتْلَىٰ عَلَيْهِمْ يَخِرُّونَ لِلْأَذْقَانِ سُجَّدًا
وَيَقُولُونَ سُبْحَانَ رَبِّنَا إِنْ كَانَ وَعْدُ رَبِّنَا لَمَفْعُولًا
وَيَخِرُّونَ لِلْأَذْقَانِ يَبْكُونَ وَيَزِيدُهُمْ خُشُوعًا

A subtle insight in repeating “they fall upon their chins”: it is mentioned first with “in prostration,” then repeated with “weeping,” as though prostration recurs as they are moved again, with weeping added the second time. And the verb “they fall” (yakhirruna) was chosen, indicating a swift fall, as though they cannot control themselves before the words of Allah. It closes with “and it increases them in humility” in the present tense: their humility keeps increasing and does not stop, whenever they recite or listen.

en.title: Until You Ascertain Welcome and Greet Their Occupants
en.excerpt: The Qur'an chose the word tasta'nisu, because the aim of seeking permission is that the people of the house feel at ease.

body.text: The verse guides the believers not to enter houses other than their own until they ascertain welcome and greet their occupants, and shows that this etiquette is better for them than entering abruptly, so that they may take heed and act upon it.
يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا لَا تَدْخُلُوا بُيُوتًا غَيْرَ بُيُوتِكُمْ حَتَّىٰ تَسْتَأْنِسُوا وَتُسَلِّمُوا عَلَىٰ أَهْلِهَا ۚ ذَٰلِكُمْ خَيْرٌ لَكُمْ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَذَكَّرُونَ

A subtle insight in the word tasta'nisu: it did not say “until you ask permission” (tasta'dhinu), but chose a word carrying the meaning of uns, ease and familiarity. The aim is that the people of the house feel reassured and at ease with the one entering, not that they be taken by surprise. In this is a lofty etiquette for visiting relatives and neighbours: choosing the right time, greeting with peace, and respecting the comfort of the household. A visit that brings ease strengthens bonds, and one that causes embarrassment weakens them.

en.title: I Have Submitted to the Lord of the Worlds
en.excerpt: Ibrahim's answer came instantly, and he did not say “I have submitted to You,” but “to the Lord of the worlds.”

body.text: The verse mentions one of the stances of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) for which Allah chose him, when his Lord commanded him to submit and surrender to Him, and his answer came in a few words. It is a short verse carrying a great meaning about obedience.
إِذۡ قَالَ لَهُۥ رَبُّهُۥٓ أَسۡلِمۡۖ قَالَ أَسۡلَمۡتُ لِرَبِّ ٱلۡعَٰلَمِينَ

A subtle insight in the answer: Ibrahim did not hesitate or ask about details; his answer came immediately: “I have submitted.” And he did not say “I have submitted to You,” but “to the Lord of the worlds,” as though declaring that submission to Allah is a duty upon all the worlds, and that he is the first of them.

In this expression is an indication that the One commanding him is the Lord of all things, so obeying Him is an honour, not a burden. Reflect on the brevity: a command of one word, “Submit,” and an answer of two words; a ready heart does not need lengthy speech.

en.title: And When I Am Ill, It Is He Who Cures Me
en.excerpt: Ibrahim attributed illness to himself and healing to his Lord, out of courtesy toward Allah.

body.text: In his dialogue with his people, Ibrahim describes his Lord: the One who created him and so guides him, who feeds him and gives him drink, and when he is ill, it is He who cures him. He lists Allah's blessings upon him in creation, guidance, food, drink and healing, acknowledging that all of it is from Him.

ٱلَّذِى خَلَقَنِى فَهُوَ يَهْدِينِ
وَٱلَّذِى هُوَ يُطْعِمُنِى وَيَسْقِينِ
وَإِذَا مَرِضْتُ فَهُوَ يَشْفِينِ

A subtle insight in the words “and when I am ill”: he said “who created me,” “who feeds me” and “who cures me,” attributing these to Allah, but he did not say “who makes me ill”; he attributed illness to himself, out of courtesy toward his Lord in attributing what is disliked. In this is a lesson in courteous speech about Allah.

And repeating the pronoun, “it is He who guides me” and “it is He who cures me,” conveys exclusivity: He alone, no other. So keep these verses on your tongue in your illness and need, and acknowledge that every good in your life comes from His creating, guiding and providing.

en.title: Then Hasten to the Remembrance of Allah
en.excerpt: Allah called the Friday prayer and its sermon “the remembrance of Allah,” to show its spirit and purpose.

body.text: Allah calls the believers, when the call to prayer is made on Friday, to hasten to it and leave off trade, and tells them that this is better for them, if only they knew. In the choice of the verse's words is a striking precision.
يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوٓا۟ إِذَا نُودِىَ لِلصَّلَوٰةِ مِن يَوْمِ ٱلْجُمُعَةِ فَٱسْعَوْا۟ إِلَىٰ ذِكْرِ ٱللَّهِ وَذَرُوا۟ ٱلْبَيْعَ ۚ ذَٰلِكُمْ خَيْرٌۭ لَّكُمْ إِن كُنتُمْ تَعْلَمُونَ

A subtle insight in the words “to the remembrance of Allah” rather than “to the prayer”: Friday is expressed by its purpose, to convey that what is intended by it is remembering Allah and being reminded of Him. Hastening here means prompt attention and care, not blameworthy rushing. Then trade is singled out to be left because it is what most occupies people at that time. And it closes with “that is better for you,” as though answering the calculation of the merchant who fears loss: leaving trade for this hour is the real profit for one who knows.

en.title: Protect Yourselves and Your Families from a Fire
en.excerpt: The verse begins with oneself before the family: the reform of a home begins with the reform of its leader.

body.text: The verse calls the believers to protect themselves and their families from a tremendous Fire whose fuel is people and stones, and describes its severity and its stern, harsh angels who do not disobey Allah in what He commands them and do what they are commanded.

يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا قُوا أَنْفُسَكُمْ وَأَهْلِيكُمْ نَارًا وَقُودُهَا النَّاسُ وَالْحِجَارَةُ عَلَيْهَا مَلَائِكَةٌ غِلَاظٌ شِدَادٌ لَا يَعْصُونَ اللَّهَ مَا أَمَرَهُمْ وَيَفْعَلُونَ مَا يُؤْمَرُونَ

A subtle insight in the order: “yourselves” comes before “your families,” because whoever has not reformed himself cannot reform others, and because example is more effective in upbringing than words. The verb “protect” (qu) comes from wiqayah, protection that precedes danger; so true upbringing is early protection through teaching, example and gentleness, not a late remedy after the mistake has happened.

en.title: But So That My Heart May Be Reassured
en.excerpt: Ibrahim distinguished between firm faith and the heart's reassurance through seeing.

body.text: Ibrahim (peace be upon him) asks his Lord to show him how He gives life to the dead, and his Lord, who knows best, asks him: Have you not believed? He gives an answer that reveals a lofty degree of certainty.

وَإِذۡ قَالَ إِبۡرَٰهِـۧمُ رَبِّ أَرِنِي كَيۡفَ تُحۡيِ ٱلۡمَوۡتَىٰۖ قَالَ أَوَلَمۡ تُؤۡمِنۖ قَالَ بَلَىٰ وَلَٰكِن لِّيَطۡمَئِنَّ قَلۡبِيۖ قَالَ فَخُذۡ أَرۡبَعَةٗ مِّنَ ٱلطَّيۡرِ فَصُرۡهُنَّ إِلَيۡكَ ثُمَّ ٱجۡعَلۡ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ جَبَلٖ مِّنۡهُنَّ جُزۡءٗا ثُمَّ ٱدۡعُهُنَّ يَأۡتِينَكَ سَعۡيٗاۚ وَٱعۡلَمۡ أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَزِيزٌ حَكِيمٞ

A subtle insight in the question: Ibrahim did not ask, “Do You give life to the dead?” but said, “Show me how” You give life to the dead. Faith in the resurrection was firm in him; he only asked to see the manner. That is why he answered “Yes,” then said, “but so that my heart may be reassured.” Certainty has degrees, and reassurance is a fruit by which faith becomes more firmly rooted. The verse closes with “that Allah is Almighty, All-Wise”: after witnessing comes the reminder of knowledge and surrender to Allah's might and wisdom.

en.title: Just as You Speak
en.excerpt: Allah swore by Himself, and likened the truth of His promise to the truth of your own speech, which you never doubt.

body.text: The two verses mention that in the heaven is people's provision and what they are promised. Then Allah swears by the Lord of the heaven and the earth that this is true beyond doubt, just as there is no doubt about their speaking when they speak.

وَفِي ٱلسَّمَآءِ رِزۡقُكُمۡ وَمَا تُوعَدُونَ
فَوَرَبِّ ٱلسَّمَآءِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضِ إِنَّهُۥ لَحَقّٞ مِّثۡلَ مَآ أَنَّكُمۡ تَنطِقُونَ

A subtle insight in the comparison with speech, “just as you speak”: He chose something every person finds in himself with certainty that needs no proof; no one doubts that he is speaking. So too should your certainty be in Allah's promise and His provision.

The verse combines the oath “By the Lord of the heaven and the earth” with the emphasis “it is surely true”: successive confirmations for a heart that may be seized by anxiety about provision and the future. So if you fear for your provision, remember this oath, then strive to seek it, reassured and confident.

en.title: And We Have Certainly Made the Qur'an Easy for Remembrance
en.excerpt: A verse repeated in Surah Al-Qamar, inviting every reader to turn toward the Qur'an.

body.text: This verse is repeated in Surah Al-Qamar after each story of the earlier nations, to remind that the Qur'an has been made easy to memorise, understand and take heed from. Then it asks: is there anyone who will take heed?
وَلَقَدْ يَسَّرْنَا الْقُرْآنَ لِلذِّكْرِ فَهَلْ مِنْ مُدَّكِرٍ

A subtle insight in the repetition: after each scene of destruction this call comes, as if it were a rest for the heart and a renewed invitation to take lesson. The emphasis with “certainly” (laqad) establishes that this ease is a fixed reality, so no one is left with an excuse for abandoning the Qur'an.

The question “so is there anyone who will take heed?” comes as a question rather than a command; it is gentler as an invitation, stirring resolve and opening the door to all who wish. If you think the Qur'an is difficult for you, remember that Allah Himself has made it easy.

en.title: An Orphan of Near Relationship
en.excerpt: Describing the orphan by kinship and the needy person by dust reveals the priorities of giving and where need lies.

body.text: Among the forms of attempting the steep path, the verses mention feeding on a day of hunger and hardship, singling out an orphan who is a relative, or a needy person clinging to the dust from the severity of his poverty.

أَوْ إِطْعَامٌ فِي يَوْمٍ ذِي مَسْغَبَةٍ
يَتِيمًا ذَا مَقْرَبَةٍ
أَوْ مِسْكِينًا ذَا مَتْرَبَةٍ

A subtle insight in the two descriptions: “of near relationship” gives the orphan two rights, the right of orphanhood and the right of kinship, so he is more deserving of being fed. And “in the dust” portrays extreme poverty in a tangible image, as though the needy person has clung to the dust. Restricting the feeding to “a day of severe hunger” indicates that giving in times of hardship carries greater reward. So begin with the orphans among your relatives, and look out for those in the greatest need.

en.title: There Is No Protector Today from the Decree of Allah
en.excerpt: The son thought the mountain would protect him, and the answer came: there is no protection except Allah's mercy.

body.text: In an awe-inspiring scene, as the ship sails through waves like mountains, Nuh (peace be upon him) calls to his son with a father's heart, inviting him to safety, and the son answers him with confidence in material means. In the dialogue is an eloquent contrast between the two speeches.

وَهِيَ تَجْرِي بِهِمْ فِي مَوْجٍ كَالْجِبَالِ وَنَادَىٰ نُوحٌ ابْنَهُ وَكَانَ فِي مَعْزِلٍ يَا بُنَيَّ ارْكَبْ مَعَنَا وَلَا تَكُنْ مَعَ الْكَافِرِينَ
قَالَ سَآوِي إِلَىٰ جَبَلٍ يَعْصِمُنِي مِنَ الْمَاءِ ۚ قَالَ لَا عَاصِمَ الْيَوْمَ مِنْ أَمْرِ اللَّهِ إِلَّا مَنْ رَحِمَ ۚ وَحَالَ بَيْنَهُمَا الْمَوْجُ فَكَانَ مِنَ الْمُغْرَقِينَ

A subtle insight in the contrast: the son said, “I will take refuge on a mountain to protect me,” and Nuh answered him, “There is no protector today... except for whom He has mercy on.” The protection he sought in the mountain is found only in Allah's mercy, and all means become void when His decree comes.

Reflect on the call “O my dear son” in the diminutive indicating compassion, then the words “and the waves came between them.” The waves were like mountains, yet they came between a father and his son in a moment. This reminds us that guidance is not inherited by lineage, but attained by responding.

en.title: He Will Be in a Pleasant Life
en.excerpt: The life itself is described as “pleased,” as though the bliss is pleased with its owner and content with him.

body.text: The two verses mention the state of one whose scales are heavy on the Day of Resurrection with righteous deeds: he will be in a life he is pleased with in Paradise. It is a great reward, contrasted in the verses after it with the state of one whose scales are light, so the difference between the two destinies becomes clear.

فَأَمَّا مَن ثَقُلَتْ مَوَٰزِينُهُۥ
فَهُوَ فِى عِيشَةٍۢ رَّاضِيَةٍۢ

A subtle insight in the words 'ishatin radiyah (a pleased life): its meaning is a pleasing life with which its owner is pleased, but the pleasure is attributed to the life itself, as an intensification of its perfection, as though it were pleased with its people. It is an Arabic style that indicates the completeness of the quality and its freedom from every impurity.

And in the expression “whose scales are heavy” is an indication that deeds have real weight on the Day of Resurrection. So never belittle a righteous deed, however small, for it may be what makes your scale heavy and brings you to that life. Do as much good as you can.

en.title: Those Who Are Heedless of Their Prayer
en.excerpt: He said “of their prayer,” not “in their prayer”: the warning is for the one heedless of it, not for one who makes a slip within it.

body.text: These two verses warn a people who pray, yet are heedless of their prayer. It is a precise description that distinguishes between two kinds of heedlessness, and every worshipper needs to pause at this difference and review himself in its light.

فَوَيْلٌۭ لِّلْمُصَلِّينَ
ٱلَّذِينَ هُمْ عَن صَلَاتِهِمْ سَاهُونَ

A subtle insight in the preposition 'an (of): heedlessness “in” the prayer happens to every worshipper, such as forgetting the number of rak'ahs, and no one is free of it. But heedlessness “of” the prayer is neglect of the prayer itself: delaying it beyond its time, treating it lightly, and not caring about it. A single preposition changed the whole meaning.

In this is mercy and warning together: mercy for one who makes a slip in his prayer while being keen on it, and a warning for one who has put prayer at the margins of his day. So be keen that your prayer is at the heart of your day, not at its edges.

en.title: They Are a Garment for You, and You Are a Garment for Them
en.excerpt: Likening spouses to a garment brings together the meanings of covering, warmth, closeness and adornment.

body.text: In the context of the rulings of fasting, Allah permitted spouses during the nights of Ramadan what had been forbidden to them before, and described the relationship between spouses beautifully: each is a garment for the other.

أُحِلَّ لَكُمۡ لَيۡلَةَ ٱلصِّيَامِ ٱلرَّفَثُ إِلَىٰ نِسَآئِكُمۡۚ هُنَّ لِبَاسٞ لَّكُمۡ وَأَنتُمۡ لِبَاسٞ لَّهُنَّۗ عَلِمَ ٱللَّهُ أَنَّكُمۡ كُنتُمۡ تَخۡتَانُونَ أَنفُسَكُمۡ فَتَابَ عَلَيۡكُمۡ وَعَفَا عَنكُمۡۖ فَٱلۡـَٰٔنَ بَٰشِرُوهُنَّ وَٱبۡتَغُواْ مَا كَتَبَ ٱللَّهُ لَكُمۡۚ وَكُلُواْ وَٱشۡرَبُواْ حَتَّىٰ يَتَبَيَّنَ لَكُمُ ٱلۡخَيۡطُ ٱلۡأَبۡيَضُ مِنَ ٱلۡخَيۡطِ ٱلۡأَسۡوَدِ مِنَ ٱلۡفَجۡرِۖ ثُمَّ أَتِمُّواْ ٱلصِّيَامَ إِلَى ٱلَّيۡلِۚ وَلَا تُبَٰشِرُوهُنَّ وَأَنتُمۡ عَٰكِفُونَ فِي ٱلۡمَسَٰجِدِۗ تِلۡكَ حُدُودُ ٱللَّهِ فَلَا تَقۡرَبُوهَاۗ كَذَٰلِكَ يُبَيِّنُ ٱللَّهُ ءَايَٰتِهِۦ لِلنَّاسِ لَعَلَّهُمۡ يَتَّقُونَ

A subtle insight in the comparison to a “garment”: a garment is the closest thing to a person; it covers him, warms him and adorns him. So too are spouses: each covers the other's faults, gives warmth and security, and is an adornment for the other among people. The expression comes reciprocally, “they are a garment for you, and you are a garment for them,” to affirm that the need and the responsibility are shared. So do not expose your partner's covering, and be warmth for them, not cold.

en.title: The Town Whose Faith Benefited It
en.excerpt: The people of Yunus (peace be upon him): a nation that returned before it was too late, so the punishment was lifted from it.

body.text: The Qur'an mentions that the towns that denied their messengers were not benefited by their faith when they saw the punishment, and it makes an exception for one people only: the people of Yunus (peace be upon him).
فَلَوْلَا كَانَتْ قَرْيَةٌ آمَنَتْ فَنَفَعَهَا إِيمَانُهَا إِلَّا قَوْمَ يُونُسَ لَمَّا آمَنُوا كَشَفْنَا عَنْهُمْ عَذَابَ الْخِزْيِ فِي الْحَيَاةِ الدُّنْيَا وَمَتَّعْنَاهُمْ إِلَىٰ حِينٍ

The people of Yunus returned sincerely to their Lord before what they had been warned of befell them, so Allah removed from them the punishment of disgrace and gave them enjoyment for a time. The lesson is that the door of repentance is open as long as there is respite in one's life, and that sincere return changes one's destiny. So do not postpone your repentance to a tomorrow that may not come; hasten while you still have the chance.

en.title: A Sign for Those Who Come After You
en.excerpt: Allah preserved Pharaoh's body after he drowned so that it would be a lesson for those after him.

body.text: When drowning overtook Pharaoh, he declared his faith, but after it was too late. Then Allah the Exalted said about his body:
فَالْيَوْمَ نُنَجِّيكَ بِبَدَنِكَ لِتَكُونَ لِمَنْ خَلْفَكَ آيَةً ۚ وَإِنَّ كَثِيرًا مِنَ النَّاسِ عَنْ آيَاتِنَا لَغَافِلُونَ

Among the subtle insights of this verse is that saving the body here is not salvation from punishment, but making the tyrant a lesson to be seen, so that no one would think that one who claimed lordship does not die. And the verse ends with a warning for every age: that many people are heedless of Allah's signs, and the lesson is present for whoever reflects.

en.title: Allah Does Not Burden a Soul Beyond Its Capacity
en.excerpt: What Allah has prescribed for you is within your capacity, and what exceeds your capacity He has lifted from you by His mercy.

body.text: When obligations weigh on you or decrees become hard upon you, remember that the One who legislated and decreed knows you better than you know yourself. He commands you only with what you can bear, and tests you only with what you can endure.

لَا يُكَلِّفُ ٱللَّهُ نَفۡسًا إِلَّا وُسۡعَهَاۚ لَهَا مَا كَسَبَتۡ وَعَلَيۡهَا مَا ٱكۡتَسَبَتۡۗ رَبَّنَا لَا تُؤَاخِذۡنَآ إِن نَّسِينَآ أَوۡ أَخۡطَأۡنَاۚ رَبَّنَا وَلَا تَحۡمِلۡ عَلَيۡنَآ إِصۡرٗا كَمَا حَمَلۡتَهُۥ عَلَى ٱلَّذِينَ مِن قَبۡلِنَاۚ رَبَّنَا وَلَا تُحَمِّلۡنَا مَا لَا طَاقَةَ لَنَا بِهِۦۖ وَٱعۡفُ عَنَّا وَٱغۡفِرۡ لَنَا وَٱرۡحَمۡنَآۚ أَنتَ مَوۡلَىٰنَا فَٱنصُرۡنَا عَلَى ٱلۡقَوۡمِ ٱلۡكَٰفِرِينَ

At the end of the verse are supplications that Allah taught us: to ask Him to pardon us for error and forgetfulness, and not to burden us with what we have no strength to bear. They are a school of hope and humility before Allah.

en.title: My Lord, Expand for Me My Chest
en.excerpt: Before every difficult task, begin by asking Allah for help.

body.text: When Musa (peace be upon him) was charged with the greatest mission, he did not begin with material preparation; he began with supplication: the expanding of his chest, the easing of his task, and eloquence of tongue.

قَالَ رَبِّ اشْرَحْ لِي صَدْرِي
وَيَسِّرْ لِي أَمْرِي
وَاحْلُلْ عُقْدَةً مِنْ لِسَانِي
يَفْقَهُوا قَوْلِي
A subtle insight we learn: the first means of success is seeking Allah's help. So make this supplication your companion before an exam, before work, and before speaking.

en.title: Change Begins Within
en.excerpt: It is Allah's way that circumstances do not change until souls change.

body.text: Many of us wait for the circumstances around us to change, and the Qur'an draws our attention to the fact that change begins in the self before it begins in reality.

لَهُ مُعَقِّبَاتٌ مِنْ بَيْنِ يَدَيْهِ وَمِنْ خَلْفِهِ يَحْفَظُونَهُ مِنْ أَمْرِ اللَّهِ ۗ إِنَّ اللَّهَ لَا يُغَيِّرُ مَا بِقَوْمٍ حَتَّىٰ يُغَيِّرُوا مَا بِأَنْفُسِهِمْ ۗ وَإِذَا أَرَادَ اللَّهُ بِقَوْمٍ سُوءًا فَلَا مَرَدَّ لَهُ ۚ وَمَا لَهُمْ مِنْ دُونِهِ مِنْ وَالٍ

If you want your state to change for the better, begin with yourself: correct your intention, guard your prayer, and leave what you know distances you from your Lord. Indeed, Allah does not let the deed of one who does good go to waste.

en.title: Has the Time Not Come for Those Who Believe?
en.excerpt: A merciful call that wakes the heart from its heedlessness before it hardens.

body.text: A verse that shakes the heart: in it is a gentle reproach from Allah to His believing servants, lest a long time pass over them and their hearts harden.

أَلَمْ يَأْنِ لِلَّذِينَ آمَنُوا أَنْ تَخْشَعَ قُلُوبُهُمْ لِذِكْرِ اللَّهِ وَمَا نَزَلَ مِنَ الْحَقِّ وَلَا يَكُونُوا كَالَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الْكِتَابَ مِنْ قَبْلُ فَطَالَ عَلَيْهِمُ الْأَمَدُ فَقَسَتْ قُلُوبُهُمْ ۖ وَكَثِيرٌ مِنْهُمْ فَاسِقُونَ

The heart is like the earth: remembrance and recitation of the Qur'an give it life, and long heedlessness hardens it. So tend your heart every day with a portion of the Book of Allah, even if it is small.

en.title: And Do Not Turn Your Cheek Away from People
en.excerpt: A wise father's advice to his son on humility and the etiquette of walking and speaking.

body.text: Among Luqman's advice to his son is guidance on bearing and conduct: not to turn his face away from people in arrogance, and not to walk with conceit.

وَلَا تُصَعِّرْ خَدَّكَ لِلنَّاسِ وَلَا تَمْشِ فِي الْأَرْضِ مَرَحًا ۖ إِنَّ اللَّهَ لَا يُحِبُّ كُلَّ مُخْتَالٍ فَخُورٍ
وَاقْصِدْ فِي مَشْيِكَ وَاغْضُضْ مِنْ صَوْتِكَ ۚ إِنَّ أَنْكَرَ الْأَصْوَاتِ لَصَوْتُ الْحَمِيرِ
A subtle insight in upbringing: humility shows in the small details, in the glance of the eye, the step of the foot, and the tone of the voice.

en.title: And the Life of This World Is Nothing but the Enjoyment of Delusion
en.excerpt: This world is a passage, not a dwelling, and the true triumph is on a Day when rewards are paid in full.

body.text: This verse sets a clear scale for success: success is not what we gather in this world, but that the servant is drawn away from the Fire and admitted to Paradise.

كُلُّ نَفْسٍ ذَائِقَةُ الْمَوْتِ ۗ وَإِنَّمَا تُوَفَّوْنَ أُجُورَكُمْ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ ۖ فَمَنْ زُحْزِحَ عَنِ النَّارِ وَأُدْخِلَ الْجَنَّةَ فَقَدْ فَازَ ۗ وَمَا الْحَيَاةُ الدُّنْيَا إِلَّا مَتَاعُ الْغُرُورِ
So keep the world in your hand, not in your heart, and use it in what brings you closer to Allah; for everything in it passes away, and righteous deeds remain.

sources: The Holy Qur'an — Surah Al Imran: 185

en.title: Those Who Restrain Anger and Pardon People
en.excerpt: A person's true strength is to control himself when angry.

body.text: Among the qualities of the God-conscious, Allah mentioned that they restrain anger and pardon people, then ended the verse by saying that He loves those who do good.
الَّذِينَ يُنْفِقُونَ فِي السَّرَّاءِ وَالضَّرَّاءِ وَالْكَاظِمِينَ الْغَيْظَ وَالْعَافِينَ عَنِ النَّاسِ ۗ وَاللَّهُ يُحِبُّ الْمُحْسِنِينَ

So if someone wrongs you, remember that pardon is elevation, not weakness; that whatever you give up for Allah's sake, Allah will replace with something better; and that Allah's love is more precious than taking revenge for oneself.

sources: The Holy Qur'an — Surah Al Imran: 134

en.title: Is the Reward for Good Anything but Good?
en.excerpt: A question whose answer lies within it: whoever does good will receive good.

body.text: This verse comes in the context of mentioning the bliss of Paradise, in the form of a question that carries the meaning of affirmation.
هَلْ جَزَاءُ الْإِحْسَانِ إِلَّا الْإِحْسَانُ
A subtle insight in the style: doing good in this world is a seed, and its fruit is a boundless goodness from Allah. So excel in your worship and with people, and you will find that with your Lord.

en.title: Avoid Much Suspicion
en.excerpt: A heart free of suspicion and backbiting is a path to a sound society.

body.text: In this verse are three instructions that protect hearts and relationships: avoiding much suspicion, refraining from spying, and refraining from backbiting.

يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا اجْتَنِبُوا كَثِيرًا مِنَ الظَّنِّ إِنَّ بَعْضَ الظَّنِّ إِثْمٌ ۖ وَلَا تَجَسَّسُوا وَلَا يَغْتَبْ بَعْضُكُمْ بَعْضًا ۚ أَيُحِبُّ أَحَدُكُمْ أَنْ يَأْكُلَ لَحْمَ أَخِيهِ مَيْتًا فَكَرِهْتُمُوهُ ۚ وَاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ ۚ إِنَّ اللَّهَ تَوَّابٌ رَحِيمٌ
The Qur'an portrays backbiting with an image that souls recoil from, so that the believer knows how ugly it is. So guard your tongue and think well of your brothers, for that is part of a pure heart.

en.title: And Tell My Servants to Say That Which Is Best
en.excerpt: A kind word builds bridges, and a hurtful word opens the doors to Satan.

body.text: Allah commanded His servants to choose the best of speech, and made clear that Satan lies in wait for the bad word, to sow discord with it among people.
وَقُلْ لِعِبَادِي يَقُولُوا الَّتِي هِيَ أَحْسَنُ ۚ إِنَّ الشَّيْطَانَ يَنْزَغُ بَيْنَهُمْ ۚ إِنَّ الشَّيْطَانَ كَانَ لِلْإِنْسَانِ عَدُوًّا مُبِينًا
So before you speak, ask yourself: is there goodness in my words? A good word is a charity to the one you speak to, and a fortress against Satan's incitement.

en.title: Repel Evil with That Which Is Better
en.excerpt: Meeting wrongdoing with goodness can turn an enemy into a friend.

body.text: This verse draws a remarkable way of dealing with others: to meet a bad deed with a good one, not with its like.
وَلَا تَسْتَوِي الْحَسَنَةُ وَلَا السَّيِّئَةُ ۚ ادْفَعْ بِالَّتِي هِيَ أَحْسَنُ فَإِذَا الَّذِي بَيْنَكَ وَبَيْنَهُ عَدَاوَةٌ كَأَنَّهُ وَلِيٌّ حَمِيمٌ

A practical subtle insight: being good to the one who wrongs you is not weakness, but a strength that dissolves enmity, and its fruit, as the verse says, is that he becomes “as though he were a devoted friend.”

en.title: Call upon Me; I Will Respond to You
en.excerpt: A promise from Allah that is never broken: whoever calls upon Him, He answers.

body.text: Supplication is an act of worship that Allah loves. He has promised to answer it, and made turning away from it a form of arrogance.
وَقَالَ رَبُّكُمُ ادْعُونِي أَسْتَجِبْ لَكُمْ ۚ إِنَّ الَّذِينَ يَسْتَكْبِرُونَ عَنْ عِبَادَتِي سَيَدْخُلُونَ جَهَنَّمَ دَاخِرِينَ
The answer may come by granting what was asked, by turning away some harm from you, or by storing up good for you. So do not be impatient, and keep knocking, for the door is never closed.

en.title: There Is No God but You; Glory Be to You
en.excerpt: A supplication with which Yunus (peace be upon him) called out in the darkness, and Allah saved him from distress.

body.text: In layers of darkness, Yunus (peace be upon him) called out to his Lord with words that combined affirming Allah's oneness, declaring His perfection, and admitting his own shortcoming.

وَذَا ٱلنُّونِ إِذ ذَّهَبَ مُغَٰضِبٗا فَظَنَّ أَن لَّن نَّقۡدِرَ عَلَيۡهِ فَنَادَىٰ فِي ٱلظُّلُمَٰتِ أَن لَّآ إِلَٰهَ إِلَّآ أَنتَ سُبۡحَٰنَكَ إِنِّي كُنتُ مِنَ ٱلظَّٰلِمِينَ
فَٱسۡتَجَبۡنَا لَهُۥ وَنَجَّيۡنَٰهُ مِنَ ٱلۡغَمِّۚ وَكَذَٰلِكَ نُـۨجِي ٱلۡمُؤۡمِنِينَ
Allah ended the story by saying, “And thus do We save the believers,” so that these words remain a refuge for every distressed person hoping for relief from his Lord.

en.title: Your Lord Has Not Forsaken You, nor Has He Detested You
en.excerpt: Reassurance for every heart that thought it was alone.

body.text: Surah Ad-Duha was revealed to reassure the heart of the Prophet ﷺ, and its message remains for every believer going through a period in which he feels distant or alone.

مَا وَدَّعَكَ رَبُّكَ وَمَا قَلَىٰ
وَلَلۡأٓخِرَةُ خَيۡرٞ لَّكَ مِنَ ٱلۡأُولَىٰ
وَلَسَوۡفَ يُعۡطِيكَ رَبُّكَ فَتَرۡضَىٰٓ
A subtle insight in the composition: Allah began by swearing by the morning brightness and the night; just as the night is followed by a radiant day, hardship is followed by relief and contentment.

en.title: So Remember Me; I Will Remember You
en.excerpt: That the King of kings should remember you... what honour could be greater than this?

body.text: Among the most wondrous things in this verse is that the reward is of the same kind as the deed, and greater than it: you remember Allah, and Allah remembers you.
فَٱذۡكُرُونِيٓ أَذۡكُرۡكُمۡ وَٱشۡكُرُواْ لِي وَلَا تَكۡفُرُونِ
So keep your tongue moist with the remembrance of Allah in all your states, and thank Him for His blessings; through remembrance and gratitude, blessings endure and the heart finds peace.

en.title: Our Lord, Let Not Our Hearts Deviate
en.excerpt: Steadfastness on guidance is a blessing to be sought, just as guidance itself is sought.

body.text: This is the supplication of those firmly grounded in knowledge: they were not deluded by their knowledge, but asked Allah for steadfastness after guidance.
رَبَّنَا لَا تُزِغْ قُلُوبَنَا بَعْدَ إِذْ هَدَيْتَنَا وَهَبْ لَنَا مِنْ لَدُنْكَ رَحْمَةً ۚ إِنَّكَ أَنْتَ الْوَهَّابُ
A subtle insight of faith: the heart turns about, and the believer, however far he has come, remains in need of Allah's making him firm. So make this supplication often.

sources: The Holy Qur'an — Surah Al Imran: 8

en.title: It Is by Mercy from Allah That You Were Gentle with Them
en.excerpt: Gentleness is the secret of hearts coming together, and consultation followed by reliance is the path to decision.

body.text: This verse shows that the Prophet's ﷺ gentleness with his Companions is a mercy from Allah, and that harshness drives people apart.

فَبِمَا رَحْمَةٍ مِنَ اللَّهِ لِنْتَ لَهُمْ ۖ وَلَوْ كُنْتَ فَظًّا غَلِيظَ الْقَلْبِ لَانْفَضُّوا مِنْ حَوْلِكَ ۖ فَاعْفُ عَنْهُمْ وَاسْتَغْفِرْ لَهُمْ وَشَاوِرْهُمْ فِي الْأَمْرِ ۖ فَإِذَا عَزَمْتَ فَتَوَكَّلْ عَلَى اللَّهِ ۚ إِنَّ اللَّهَ يُحِبُّ الْمُتَوَكِّلِينَ

A subtle insight in the order of the verse: pardon, then seeking forgiveness, then consultation, then resolve and reliance on Allah; a complete method for anyone who takes charge of any matter, even a small one.

sources: The Holy Qur'an — Surah Al Imran: 159

en.title: Indeed, with Hardship Comes Ease
en.excerpt: Whenever difficulty intensifies, know that Allah's relief is near; one hardship will never overcome two eases.

body.text: Among Allah's ways in His creation is that He brings ease after hardship and abundance after constraint. No matter becomes tight without relief folded within it, and no crisis intensifies without its resolution drawing near.

فَإِنَّ مَعَ الْعُسْرِ يُسْرًا
إِنَّ مَعَ الْعُسْرِ يُسْرًا

Allah repeated the mention of ease with hardship. Many of the scholars of tafsir held that “hardship” comes with the definite article in both places, so it is one, while “ease” comes indefinite, so it is multiple; and one hardship will never overcome two eases.
So when distress befalls you, think well of your Lord, and stay at His door with supplication and patience; for however long the night may be, the dawn is coming, by Allah's permission.

en.title: In the Remembrance of Allah Do Hearts Find Rest
en.excerpt: Hearts do not settle or find calm except through remembrance of their Creator and Master.

body.text: Hearts are by nature prone to anxiety and fluctuation, and they find no rest until they return to their Lord. Remembrance is the nourishment of souls; through it chests are expanded and worries are lifted.
الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَتَطْمَئِنُّ قُلُوبُهُمْ بِذِكْرِ اللَّهِ ۗ أَلَا بِذِكْرِ اللَّهِ تَطْمَئِنُّ الْقُلُوبُ

Whoever wants a tranquility untouched by sorrow should remember Allah often in his day: glorifying, praising, seeking forgiveness, and reciting His Book. The more the tongue is devoted to remembrance, the more the heart finds intimacy with its Lord.

en.title: Seek Help Through Patience and Prayer
en.excerpt: When trials intensify, there is no refuge like patience and no help like prayer.

body.text: Allah has given the believer, in times of hardship, two great doors to flee to: patience, which holds the soul back from panic, and prayer, which connects him to his Lord and supplies him with strength and tranquility.
يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ ٱسۡتَعِينُواْ بِٱلصَّبۡرِ وَٱلصَّلَوٰةِۚ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ مَعَ ٱلصَّٰبِرِينَ

And at the end of the verse is great glad tidings: Allah is with the patient. Whoever is patient, Allah is with him with protection and support, and Allah's company is enough as honour and consolation.

en.title: Indeed, I Am Near
en.excerpt: A door that is never closed, and a Lord who is near and answers whoever calls upon Him.

body.text: Among the greatest comforts for a servant in his loneliness and distress is to know that his Lord is near to him, hearing his supplication and answering his call, with no need of any intermediary.
وَإِذَا سَأَلَكَ عِبَادِي عَنِّي فَإِنِّي قَرِيبٌۖ أُجِيبُ دَعۡوَةَ ٱلدَّاعِ إِذَا دَعَانِۖ فَلۡيَسۡتَجِيبُواْ لِي وَلۡيُؤۡمِنُواْ بِي لَعَلَّهُمۡ يَرۡشُدُونَ

So be persistent in supplicating to your Lord, think well of His answer, and respond to Him yourself through obedience. Supplication is worship in itself, and whoever knocks at the door of the Most Generous will never be disappointed.

en.title: Do Not Despair of the Mercy of Allah
en.excerpt: However great the sins, Allah's mercy is wider, and His door is open to those who repent.

body.text: A sin may weigh so heavily on the heart that its owner thinks his door has been closed. Here comes the merciful call that opens the door of hope for the servant, however much he has transgressed against himself.
قُلْ يَا عِبَادِيَ الَّذِينَ أَسْرَفُوا عَلَىٰ أَنْفُسِهِمْ لَا تَقْنَطُوا مِنْ رَحْمَةِ اللَّهِ ۚ إِنَّ اللَّهَ يَغْفِرُ الذُّنُوبَ جَمِيعًا ۚ إِنَّهُ هُوَ الْغَفُورُ الرَّحِيمُ
So hasten to sincere repentance, and follow a bad deed with a good one to erase it. It is from Allah's mercy that He made repentance a way by which the servant returns to Him whenever his foot slips.

en.title: If You Are Grateful, I Will Surely Increase You
en.excerpt: Gratitude secures the blessings you have and draws in the blessings you lack.

body.text: Blessings endure and increase through gratitude, and vanish and decrease through ingratitude. No blessing is preserved like gratitude for it, and no missing blessing is drawn in like praising Allah for it.
وَإِذْ تَأَذَّنَ رَبُّكُمْ لَئِنْ شَكَرْتُمْ لَأَزِيدَنَّكُمْ ۖ وَلَئِنْ كَفَرْتُمْ إِنَّ عَذَابِي لَشَدِيدٌ
So keep your tongue moist with praise of Allah, your heart acknowledging His favour, and your limbs working in His obedience; that is the complete gratitude that brings increase.

en.title: And Whoever Is Mindful of Allah, He Will Make for Him a Way Out
en.excerpt: Taqwa is a way out of every difficulty, and reliance on Allah is sufficiency against every worry.

body.text: Whoever deals with Allah with taqwa in private and in public, Allah guarantees him relief from where he does not expect, and provides for him through doors that never crossed his mind.

وَمَنْ يَتَّقِ اللَّهَ يَجْعَلْ لَهُ مَخْرَجًا
وَيَرْزُقْهُ مِنْ حَيْثُ لَا يَحْتَسِبُ ۚ وَمَنْ يَتَوَكَّلْ عَلَى اللَّهِ فَهُوَ حَسْبُهُ
So combine taqwa with reliance: take the lawful means, then entrust your affair to Allah, confident in His sufficiency; whoever has Allah as his sufficiency, nothing will harm him.

en.title: And to Parents, Good Treatment
en.excerpt: Honouring parents is one of the greatest doors of Paradise, so do not close it on yourself.

body.text: Allah joined honouring parents with affirming His oneness and worshipping Him, indicating the greatness of their right, and that being good to them is among the noblest acts that bring one close to Allah, especially in their old age and weakness.

وَقَضَىٰ رَبُّكَ أَلَّا تَعْبُدُوا إِلَّا إِيَّاهُ وَبِالْوَالِدَيْنِ إِحْسَانًا ۚ إِمَّا يَبْلُغَنَّ عِنْدَكَ الْكِبَرَ أَحَدُهُمَا أَوْ كِلَاهُمَا فَلَا تَقُلْ لَهُمَا أُفٍّ وَلَا تَنْهَرْهُمَا وَقُلْ لَهُمَا قَوْلًا كَرِيمًا
وَاخْفِضْ لَهُمَا جَنَاحَ الذُّلِّ مِنَ الرَّحْمَةِ وَقُلْ رَبِّ ارْحَمْهُمَا كَمَا رَبَّيَانِي صَغِيرًا

So be gentle with them in your words, lower your wing to them, and pray for them in their lifetime and after their death. Allah's pleasure lies in their pleasure, and your dutifulness to them is a cause of your children's dutifulness to you.
